# ============================================
# Task 7: Imbalanced Sampling with RDD
# ============================================

from pyspark.sql.functions import col, when, count, lit, length
from pyspark.sql.types import IntegerType, StringType
from collections import Counter
import numpy as np
import builtins  # Add this to access Python's built-in min/max

# Preserve Python's built-in min/max (recommended for clarity)
python_min = builtins.min
python_max = builtins.max
python_sum = builtins.sum  # ADD THIS LINE

print("=" * 60)
print("Task 7: Imbalanced Sampling with RDD")
print("=" * 60)

# Check if feature-enriched dataframe exists, otherwise use cleaned dataframe
if 'df_wikicorpus_with_features' in globals() and df_wikicorpus_with_features is not None:
    df_source = df_wikicorpus_with_features
    print("\n✓ Using feature-enriched dataframe from Task 4")
elif 'df_wikicorpus' in globals() and df_wikicorpus is not None:
    df_source = df_wikicorpus
    print("\n✓ Using cleaned wikicorpus dataframe")
    print("  Note: For better imbalance analysis, run Task 4 first to extract features")
else:
    print("\n✗ Error: No dataframe available. Please load and clean the dataset first.")
    df_source = None

if df_source is not None:
    # ============================================
    # STEP 1: Identify Imbalanced Classes
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 1: Identifying Imbalanced Classes")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    # Create binary classification labels based on extracted features
    # We'll use multiple criteria to demonstrate different imbalance scenarios
    
    # Criterion 1: Articles with dates vs without dates (using features from Task 4)
    if 'date_features' in [field.name for field in df_source.schema.fields]:
        print("\nCriterion 1: Articles with dates vs without dates")
        df_with_labels = df_source.withColumn(
            "has_dates",
            when(col("date_features.count") > 0, 1).otherwise(0)
        )
    else:
        # Fallback: Use text length as proxy
        print("\nCriterion 1: Articles with long text vs short text (fallback)")
        df_with_labels = df_source.withColumn(
            "text_length",
            when(col("text").isNotNull(), length(col("text"))).otherwise(0)
        ).withColumn(
            "has_dates",
            when(col("text_length") > 1000, 1).otherwise(0)
        )
    
    # Criterion 2: Articles with identifiers (ISBN/URL/Email) vs without
    if 'identifier_features' in [field.name for field in df_source.schema.fields]:
        df_with_labels = df_with_labels.withColumn(
            "has_identifiers",
            when(
                (col("identifier_features.isbn_count") > 0) |
                (col("identifier_features.url_count") > 0) |
                (col("identifier_features.email_count") > 0),
                1
            ).otherwise(0)
        )
    else:
        df_with_labels = df_with_labels.withColumn("has_identifiers", lit(0))
    
    # Criterion 3: Articles with high feature richness (multiple feature types)
    if 'date_features' in [field.name for field in df_source.schema.fields]:
        df_with_labels = df_with_labels.withColumn(
            "feature_richness",
            col("date_features.count") + 
            col("identifier_features.isbn_count") + 
            col("identifier_features.url_count") +
            col("nested_tag_features.link_count")
        ).withColumn(
            "is_feature_rich",
            when(col("feature_richness") >= 10, 1).otherwise(0)
        )
    else:
        df_with_labels = df_with_labels.withColumn("is_feature_rich", lit(0))
    
    # Show class distribution BEFORE sampling
    print("\n" + "-" * 60)
    print("BEFORE SAMPLING - Class Distribution Analysis")
    print("-" * 60)
    
    # Distribution for "has_dates" class
    date_distribution = df_with_labels.groupBy("has_dates").agg(count("*").alias("count")).collect()
    total_rows = df_with_labels.count()
    
    print("\n1. Date-based Classification (has_dates):")
    date_counts = {row['has_dates']: row['count'] for row in date_distribution}
    for label in [0, 1]:
        count_label = date_counts.get(label, 0)
        percentage = (count_label / total_rows * 100) if total_rows > 0 else 0
        print(f"   Class {label} (has_dates={label}): {count_label:,} rows ({percentage:.2f}%)")
    
    # Calculate imbalance ratio
    if 0 in date_counts and 1 in date_counts:
        count_0 = date_counts[0]
        count_1 = date_counts[1]
        minority_class_count = python_min(count_0, count_1)
        majority_class_count = python_max(count_0, count_1)
        imbalance_ratio = majority_class_count / minority_class_count if minority_class_count > 0 else float('inf')
        print(f"   Imbalance Ratio: {imbalance_ratio:.2f}:1 (majority:minority)")
    
    # Distribution for "has_identifiers" class
    identifier_distribution = df_with_labels.groupBy("has_identifiers").agg(count("*").alias("count")).collect()
    print("\n2. Identifier-based Classification (has_identifiers):")
    identifier_counts = {row['has_identifiers']: row['count'] for row in identifier_distribution}
    for label in [0, 1]:
        count_label = identifier_counts.get(label, 0)
        percentage = (count_label / total_rows * 100) if total_rows > 0 else 0
        print(f"   Class {label} (has_identifiers={label}): {count_label:,} rows ({percentage:.2f}%)")
    
    if 0 in identifier_counts and 1 in identifier_counts:
        count_0 = identifier_counts[0]
        count_1 = identifier_counts[1]
        minority_class_count_id = python_min(count_0, count_1)
        majority_class_count_id = python_max(count_0, count_1)
        imbalance_ratio_id = majority_class_count_id / minority_class_count_id if minority_class_count_id > 0 else float('inf')
        print(f"   Imbalance Ratio: {imbalance_ratio_id:.2f}:1 (majority:minority)")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 2: Convert to RDD for Sampling Operations
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 2: Converting to RDD for Sampling Operations")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    # Convert DataFrame to RDD with key-value pairs
    # Key: class label, Value: row data
    rdd_with_keys = df_with_labels.rdd.map(
        lambda row: (row['has_dates'], row)
    )
    
    print(f"\n✓ Converted DataFrame to RDD")
    print(f"  Total partitions: {rdd_with_keys.getNumPartitions()}")
    print(f"  Total records: {rdd_with_keys.count():,}")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 3: Statistical Analysis of Imbalance
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 3: Statistical Analysis of Imbalance")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    # Count records per class using RDD operations
    class_counts_rdd = rdd_with_keys.map(lambda x: (x[0], 1)).reduceByKey(lambda a, b: a + b)
    class_counts = dict(class_counts_rdd.collect())
    
    print("\nClass distribution (from RDD):")
    for label in sorted(class_counts.keys()):
        count_label = class_counts[label]
        percentage = (count_label / total_rows * 100) if total_rows > 0 else 0
        print(f"  Class {label}: {count_label:,} ({percentage:.2f}%)")
    
    # Calculate statistical measures
    if len(class_counts) == 2:
        class_0_count = class_counts.get(0, 0)
        class_1_count = class_counts.get(1, 0)
        
        # Imbalance ratio
        if class_0_count > 0 and class_1_count > 0:
            if class_0_count > class_1_count:
                imbalance_ratio = class_0_count / class_1_count
                majority_class = 0
                minority_class = 1
            else:
                imbalance_ratio = class_1_count / class_0_count
                majority_class = 1
                minority_class = 0
            
            print(f"\nStatistical Summary:")
            print(f"  Majority Class: {majority_class} ({python_max(class_0_count, class_1_count):,} records)")
            print(f"  Minority Class: {minority_class} ({python_min(class_0_count, class_1_count):,} records)")
            print(f"  Imbalance Ratio: {imbalance_ratio:.2f}:1")
            print(f"  Minority Class Percentage: {(python_min(class_0_count, class_1_count)/total_rows*100):.2f}%")
            
            # Justification for sampling approach
            print(f"\nJustification for Sampling Strategy:")
            if imbalance_ratio > 2.0:
                print(f"  • Imbalance ratio ({imbalance_ratio:.2f}:1) exceeds 2:1 threshold")
                print(f"  • Minority class represents {(python_min(class_0_count, class_1_count)/total_rows*100):.2f}% of data")
                print(f"  • Recommended: Oversampling minority class or undersampling majority class")
                print(f"  • Strategy: Stratified sampling to balance classes")
            else:
                print(f"  • Moderate imbalance detected ({imbalance_ratio:.2f}:1)")
                print(f"  • Strategy: Light oversampling of minority class")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 4: Implement RDD-based Sampling Strategies
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 4: Implementing RDD-based Sampling Strategies")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    # Strategy 1: Stratified Random Sampling (proportional)
    print("\nStrategy 1: Stratified Random Sampling (Proportional)")
    print("-" * 60)
    
    # Calculate sampling fractions for each class
    # Target: 50-50 split (balanced)
    target_size_per_class = python_min(*class_counts.values()) if class_counts else 0
    sampling_fractions = {}
    
    for label, count in class_counts.items():
        if count > 0:
            # For majority class: undersample to match minority
            # For minority class: keep all (or slight oversample)
            if count == python_max(*class_counts.values()):
                # Majority class - undersample
                fraction = target_size_per_class / count
                sampling_fractions[label] = python_min(fraction, 1.0)  # Cap at 1.0
            else:
                # Minority class - keep all
                sampling_fractions[label] = 1.0
        else:
            sampling_fractions[label] = 0.0
    
    print(f"Sampling fractions: {sampling_fractions}")
    
    # Apply stratified sampling using RDD sampleByKey
    # Note: sampleByKey requires fractions as a dict
    sampled_rdd_stratified = rdd_with_keys.sampleByKey(
        withReplacement=False,
        fractions=sampling_fractions,
        seed=42
    )
    
    # Count results
    sampled_counts_stratified = dict(
        sampled_rdd_stratified.map(lambda x: (x[0], 1))
        .reduceByKey(lambda a, b: a + b)
        .collect()
    )
    
    total_sampled = python_sum(sampled_counts_stratified.values())
    
    print(f"\nAfter Stratified Sampling:")
    for label in sorted(sampled_counts_stratified.keys()):
        count_label = sampled_counts_stratified[label]
        percentage = (count_label / total_sampled * 100) if total_sampled > 0 else 0
        print(f"  Class {label}: {count_label:,} ({percentage:.2f}%)")
    
    # Strategy 2: Custom Filtering with Key-based Logic
    print("\n" + "-" * 60)
    print("Strategy 2: Custom Filtering with Key-based Logic (Oversampling)")
    print("-" * 60)
    
    # Separate classes
    minority_class_label = python_min(class_counts, key=class_counts.get)
    majority_class_label = python_max(class_counts, key=class_counts.get)
    
    minority_rdd = rdd_with_keys.filter(lambda x: x[0] == minority_class_label)
    majority_rdd = rdd_with_keys.filter(lambda x: x[0] == majority_class_label)
    
    minority_count = minority_rdd.count()
    majority_count = majority_rdd.count()
    
    print(f"Minority class ({minority_class_label}): {minority_count:,} records")
    print(f"Majority class ({majority_class_label}): {majority_count:,} records")
    
    # Oversample minority class by duplicating with replacement
    # Target: Match majority class size
    if minority_count > 0 and majority_count > 0:
        oversample_factor = majority_count / minority_count
        num_samples_needed = int(majority_count - minority_count)
        
        # Sample with replacement from minority class
        minority_oversampled = minority_rdd.sample(
            withReplacement=True,
            fraction=oversample_factor,
            seed=42
        )
        
        # Combine: original minority + oversampled minority + all majority
        balanced_rdd = minority_rdd.union(minority_oversampled).union(majority_rdd)
        
        # Count results
        balanced_counts = dict(
            balanced_rdd.map(lambda x: (x[0], 1))
            .reduceByKey(lambda a, b: a + b)
            .collect()
        )
        
        total_balanced = python_sum(balanced_counts.values())
        
        print(f"\nAfter Oversampling (Custom Filtering):")
        print(f"  Oversample factor: {oversample_factor:.2f}x")
        print(f"  Additional samples: {num_samples_needed:,}")
        for label in sorted(balanced_counts.keys()):
            count_label = balanced_counts[label]
            percentage = (count_label / total_balanced * 100) if total_balanced > 0 else 0
            print(f"  Class {label}: {count_label:,} ({percentage:.2f}%)")
        
        # Calculate new imbalance ratio
        if len(balanced_counts) == 2:
            new_minority_count = python_min(*balanced_counts.values())
            new_majority_count = python_max(*balanced_counts.values())
            new_imbalance_ratio = new_majority_count / new_minority_count if new_minority_count > 0 else float('inf')
            print(f"  New Imbalance Ratio: {new_imbalance_ratio:.2f}:1")
    
    # Strategy 3: Weighted Sampling based on Feature Richness
    print("\n" + "-" * 60)
    print("Strategy 3: Weighted Sampling (Feature-based)")
    print("-" * 60)
    
    # Create weighted keys: (class_label, weight_based_on_features)
    if "feature_richness" in [field.name for field in df_with_labels.schema.fields]:
        weighted_rdd = df_with_labels.rdd.map(
            lambda row: (
                row['has_dates'],
                (row, row['feature_richness'] if row['feature_richness'] else 0)
            )
        )
        
        # Sample with higher probability for feature-rich articles
        # Use feature richness as weight
        if not weighted_rdd.isEmpty():
            max_richness = weighted_rdd.map(lambda x: x[1][1]).max()
        else:
            max_richness = 0
        
        # Normalize weights and create sampling probabilities
        weighted_with_prob = weighted_rdd.map(
            lambda x: (
                x[0],
                (x[1][0], 0.5 + 0.5 * (x[1][1] / max_richness) if max_richness > 0 else 0.5)
            )
        )
        
        # Sample based on weights (higher weight = higher probability)
        # This is a simplified approach - in practice, you'd use more sophisticated methods
        sampled_weighted = weighted_with_prob.filter(
            lambda x: np.random.random() < x[1][1]
        )
        
        weighted_counts = dict(
            sampled_weighted.map(lambda x: (x[0], 1))
            .reduceByKey(lambda a, b: a + b)
            .collect()
        )
        
        total_weighted = python_sum(weighted_counts.values())
        
        print(f"\nAfter Weighted Sampling (Feature-based):")
        for label in sorted(weighted_counts.keys()):
            count_label = weighted_counts[label]
            percentage = (count_label / total_weighted * 100) if total_weighted > 0 else 0
            print(f"  Class {label}: {count_label:,} ({percentage:.2f}%)")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 5: Compare Before/After Distributions
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 5: Before/After Distribution Comparison")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("BEFORE SAMPLING")
    print("=" * 60)
    print(f"Total records: {total_rows:,}")
    for label in sorted(class_counts.keys()):
        count_label = class_counts[label]
        percentage = (count_label / total_rows * 100) if total_rows > 0 else 0
        print(f"  Class {label}: {count_label:,} ({percentage:.2f}%)")
    
    if len(class_counts) == 2:
        class_val_list = list(class_counts.values())
        old_imbalance = python_max(class_val_list) / python_min(class_val_list) if python_min(class_val_list) > 0 else float('inf')
        print(f"  Imbalance Ratio: {old_imbalance:.2f}:1")
    
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("AFTER STRATIFIED SAMPLING")
    print("=" * 60)
    print(f"Total records: {total_sampled:,}")
    for label in sorted(sampled_counts_stratified.keys()):
        count_label = sampled_counts_stratified[label]
        percentage = (count_label / total_sampled * 100) if total_sampled > 0 else 0
        print(f"  Class {label}: {count_label:,} ({percentage:.2f}%)")
    
    if len(sampled_counts_stratified) == 2:
        sampled_val_list = list(sampled_counts_stratified.values())
        new_imbalance = python_max(sampled_val_list) / python_min(sampled_val_list) if python_min(sampled_val_list) > 0 else float('inf')
        print(f"  Imbalance Ratio: {new_imbalance:.2f}:1")
        improvement = ((old_imbalance - new_imbalance) / old_imbalance * 100) if (old_imbalance and old_imbalance > 0) else 0
        print(f"  Improvement: {improvement:.2f}% reduction in imbalance")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 6: Convert Sampled RDD back to DataFrame
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 6: Converting Sampled RDD to DataFrame")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    # Extract row data from key-value pairs
    sampled_rows_rdd = sampled_rdd_stratified.map(lambda x: x[1])
    
    # Get schema from original dataframe
    sampled_schema = df_with_labels.schema
    
    # Convert to DataFrame
    df_sampled = spark.createDataFrame(sampled_rows_rdd, sampled_schema)
    
    print(f"\n✓ Converted sampled RDD to DataFrame")
    print(f"  Original rows: {total_rows:,}")
    print(f"  Sampled rows: {df_sampled.count():,}")
    print(f"  Reduction: {((total_rows - df_sampled.count()) / total_rows * 100):.2f}%")
    
    # Cache for future use
    df_sampled.cache()
    
    # Show sample of sampled data
    print(f"\nSample of sampled data:")
    df_sampled.select("id", "title", "has_dates", "has_identifiers").show(10, truncate=False)
    
    # ============================================
    # SUMMARY
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("TASK 7 SUMMARY: Imbalanced Sampling with RDD")
    print("=" * 60)
    print("\n✓ Identified imbalanced classes using extracted features")
    print("✓ Implemented multiple RDD-based sampling strategies:")
    print("  • Stratified random sampling (sampleByKey)")
    print("  • Custom filtering with oversampling")
    print("  • Weighted sampling based on feature richness")
    print("✓ Demonstrated before/after distribution effects")
    print("✓ Provided statistical justification for sampling approach")
    print("✓ Used RDD transformations: map, filter, sampleByKey, reduceByKey, union")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    # Store sampled dataframe for future use
    df_wikicorpus_sampled = df_sampled

# ============================================
# Task 18: Data Validation and Checkpointing
# ============================================

from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, when, length, isnan, isnull, trim, lit
from pyspark.sql.types import StructType, StructField, StringType, IntegerType, BooleanType
from pyspark import StorageLevel
import time
import os

print("=" * 60)
print("Task 18: Data Validation and Checkpointing")
print("=" * 60)

# Check if dataframe exists
if 'df_wikicorpus' in globals() and df_wikicorpus is not None:
    df_source = df_wikicorpus
    print("\n✓ Using cleaned wikicorpus dataframe")
elif 'df_wikicorpus_cleaned' in globals() and df_wikicorpus_cleaned is not None:
    df_source = df_wikicorpus_cleaned
    print("\n✓ Using cleaned wikicorpus dataframe")
else:
    print("\n✗ Error: No dataframe available. Please load and clean the dataset first.")
    df_source = None

if df_source is not None:
    # ============================================
    # STEP 1: Define Data Quality Constraints
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 1: Defining Data Quality Constraints")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    # Define schema constraints
    EXPECTED_SCHEMA = StructType([
        StructField("id", StringType(), nullable=False),
        StructField("title", StringType(), nullable=False),
        StructField("text", StringType(), nullable=False)
    ])
    
    # Define value range constraints
    CONSTRAINTS = {
        "id": {
            "non_null": True,
            "non_empty": True,
            "min_length": 1,
            "max_length": 100,
            "pattern": r'^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$'  # Alphanumeric, underscore, hyphen
        },
        "title": {
            "non_null": True,
            "non_empty": True,
            "min_length": 1,
            "max_length": 500,
            "pattern": None  # No specific pattern required
        },
        "text": {
            "non_null": True,
            "non_empty": True,
            "min_length": 10,  # Minimum text length
            "max_length": 1000000,  # Maximum text length (1MB)
            "pattern": None
        }
    }
    
    print("\nDefined data quality constraints:")
    print("  ✓ Schema compliance: 3 required columns (id, title, text)")
    print("  ✓ Non-null constraints: All columns must be non-null")
    print("  ✓ Value range constraints:")
    print("    - id: 1-100 characters, alphanumeric pattern")
    print("    - title: 1-500 characters")
    print("    - text: 10-1,000,000 characters")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 2: Schema Compliance Validation
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 2: Schema Compliance Validation")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    # Check if schema matches expected schema
    actual_schema = df_source.schema
    expected_fields = {field.name: field.dataType for field in EXPECTED_SCHEMA.fields}
    actual_fields = {field.name: field.dataType for field in actual_schema.fields}
    
    schema_compliant = True
    schema_issues = []
    
    print("\nSchema validation:")
    for field_name, expected_type in expected_fields.items():
        if field_name not in actual_fields:
            schema_compliant = False
            schema_issues.append(f"Missing column: {field_name}")
            print(f"  ✗ Missing column: {field_name}")
        elif str(actual_fields[field_name]) != str(expected_type):
            schema_compliant = False
            schema_issues.append(f"Type mismatch for {field_name}: expected {expected_type}, got {actual_fields[field_name]}")
            print(f"  ✗ Type mismatch: {field_name} (expected {expected_type}, got {actual_fields[field_name]})")
        else:
            print(f"  ✓ Column '{field_name}': type matches ({expected_type})")
    
    if schema_compliant:
        print("\n✓ Schema compliance: PASSED")
    else:
        print(f"\n✗ Schema compliance: FAILED")
        print(f"  Issues: {schema_issues}")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 3: Data Constraint Validation
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 3: Data Constraint Validation")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    # Create validation functions
    def validate_non_null(df, column_name):
        """Check non-null constraint"""
        null_count = df.filter(col(column_name).isNull()).count()
        return null_count == 0, null_count
    
    def validate_non_empty(df, column_name):
        """Check non-empty constraint"""
        empty_count = df.filter(
            (col(column_name).isNull()) | 
            (trim(col(column_name)) == "") |
            (length(trim(col(column_name))) == 0)
        ).count()
        return empty_count == 0, empty_count
    
    def validate_length_range(df, column_name, min_len, max_len):
        """Check length range constraint"""
        invalid_count = df.filter(
            (length(col(column_name)) < min_len) |
            (length(col(column_name)) > max_len)
        ).count()
        return invalid_count == 0, invalid_count
    
    def validate_pattern(df, column_name, pattern):
        """Check pattern constraint using regex"""
        if pattern is None:
            return True, 0
        
        from pyspark.sql.functions import regexp_extract
        invalid_count = df.filter(
            regexp_extract(col(column_name), pattern, 0) == ""
        ).count()
        return invalid_count == 0, invalid_count
    
    # Perform validation checks
    validation_results = {}
    total_rows = df_source.count()
    
    print(f"\nValidating {total_rows:,} rows against constraints...")
    
    for column_name, constraints in CONSTRAINTS.items():
        print(f"\nValidating column: {column_name}")
        column_results = {}
        
        # Non-null check
        if constraints.get("non_null", False):
            is_valid, count = validate_non_null(df_source, column_name)
            column_results["non_null"] = {"valid": is_valid, "violations": count}
            status = "✓" if is_valid else "✗"
            print(f"  {status} Non-null: {count:,} violations")
        
        # Non-empty check
        if constraints.get("non_empty", False):
            is_valid, count = validate_non_empty(df_source, column_name)
            column_results["non_empty"] = {"valid": is_valid, "violations": count}
            status = "✓" if is_valid else "✗"
            print(f"  {status} Non-empty: {count:,} violations")
        
        # Length range check
        if "min_length" in constraints or "max_length" in constraints:
            min_len = constraints.get("min_length", 0)
            max_len = constraints.get("max_length", float('inf'))
            is_valid, count = validate_length_range(df_source, column_name, min_len, max_len)
            column_results["length_range"] = {"valid": is_valid, "violations": count, "min": min_len, "max": max_len}
            status = "✓" if is_valid else "✗"
            print(f"  {status} Length range ({min_len}-{max_len}): {count:,} violations")
        
        # Pattern check
        if constraints.get("pattern"):
            is_valid, count = validate_pattern(df_source, column_name, constraints["pattern"])
            column_results["pattern"] = {"valid": is_valid, "violations": count}
            status = "✓" if is_valid else "✗"
            print(f"  {status} Pattern match: {count:,} violations")
        
        validation_results[column_name] = column_results
    
    # Overall validation summary
    all_valid = all(
        all(check["valid"] for check in column_results.values())
        for column_results in validation_results.values()
    )
    
    print("\n" + "-" * 60)
    print("Overall Validation Summary")
    print("-" * 60)
    if all_valid:
        print("✓ All constraints satisfied")
    else:
        print("✗ Some constraints violated")
        for column_name, column_results in validation_results.items():
            for check_name, check_result in column_results.items():
                if not check_result["valid"]:
                    print(f"  - {column_name}.{check_name}: {check_result['violations']:,} violations")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 4: Set Up Checkpointing Directory
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 4: Setting Up Checkpointing")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    # Set checkpoint directory
    checkpoint_dir = "./checkpoints/data_quality"
    os.makedirs(checkpoint_dir, exist_ok=True)
    
    # Set Spark checkpoint directory
    sc.setCheckpointDir(checkpoint_dir)
    
    print(f"\n✓ Checkpoint directory configured: {os.path.abspath(checkpoint_dir)}")
    print("  Checkpointing enables fault-tolerance by saving RDD lineage")
    print("  to disk, allowing recovery from failures without recomputing")
    print("  the entire transformation chain.")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 5: Iterative Process with Checkpointing
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 5: Iterative Process with Checkpointing")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    # Simulate an iterative data quality improvement process
    # This mimics a while loop that processes data in batches and validates iteratively
    
    print("\nSimulating iterative data quality improvement process...")
    print("This demonstrates checkpointing in an iterative scenario.")
    
    # Convert to RDD for iterative processing
    rdd_source = df_source.rdd
    
    # Define iterative quality improvement function
    def iterative_quality_improvement(rdd, max_iterations=5, quality_threshold=0.95):
        """
        Iterative process that improves data quality through multiple passes.
        Uses checkpointing to break lineage and enable fault-tolerance.
        """
        iteration = 0
        current_rdd = rdd
        quality_scores = []
        
        print(f"\nStarting iterative quality improvement...")
        print(f"  Max iterations: {max_iterations}")
        print(f"  Quality threshold: {quality_threshold*100:.1f}%")
        
        while iteration < max_iterations:
            iteration += 1
            print(f"\n--- Iteration {iteration} ---")
            
            # Perform quality checks and filtering
            # Filter out rows that don't meet quality criteria
            def quality_filter(row):
                """Filter function for quality improvement"""
                try:
                    # Check if row has required attributes
                    if not hasattr(row, 'id') or not hasattr(row, 'title') or not hasattr(row, 'text'):
                        return False
                    
                    # Validate id
                    if not row.id or len(str(row.id).strip()) < 1 or len(str(row.id)) > 100:
                        return False
                    
                    # Validate title
                    if not row.title or len(str(row.title).strip()) < 1 or len(str(row.title)) > 500:
                        return False
                    
                    # Validate text
                    if not row.text or len(str(row.text).strip()) < 10:
                        return False
                    
                    return True
                except:
                    return False
            
            # Apply quality filter
            filtered_rdd = current_rdd.filter(quality_filter)
            
            # Checkpoint every 2 iterations to break lineage
            if iteration % 2 == 0:
                print(f"  Checkpointing at iteration {iteration}...")
                filtered_rdd.checkpoint()
                # Force computation to materialize checkpoint
                sample_count = filtered_rdd.take(1)
                print(f"  ✓ Checkpoint created (lineage broken)")
            
            # Calculate quality score
            total_count = current_rdd.count()
            filtered_count = filtered_rdd.count()
            quality_score = filtered_count / total_count if total_count > 0 else 0
            quality_scores.append(quality_score)
            
            print(f"  Total rows: {total_count:,}")
            print(f"  Valid rows: {filtered_count:,}")
            print(f"  Quality score: {quality_score*100:.2f}%")
            
            # Update current RDD
            current_rdd = filtered_rdd
            
            # Check if quality threshold reached
            if quality_score >= quality_threshold:
                print(f"\n✓ Quality threshold reached at iteration {iteration}")
                break
        
        return current_rdd, quality_scores
    
    # Run iterative process
    start_time = time.time()
    improved_rdd, quality_history = iterative_quality_improvement(rdd_source, max_iterations=3, quality_threshold=0.90)
    elapsed_time = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"\n✓ Iterative process completed in {elapsed_time:.2f} seconds")
    print(f"  Quality improvement history: {[f'{q*100:.1f}%' for q in quality_history]}")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 6: Demonstrate Fault Tolerance
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 6: Demonstrating Fault Tolerance with Checkpointing")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    print("\nFault Tolerance Explanation:")
    print("=" * 60)
    print("""
Checkpointing plays a critical role in fault-tolerance for iterative processes:

1. **Lineage Breaking**: 
   - Without checkpointing, Spark maintains the entire RDD lineage (transformation history)
   - Long lineages can cause stack overflow errors and slow recovery
   - Checkpointing saves RDD to disk and breaks the lineage chain

2. **Failure Recovery**:
   - If a node fails during computation, Spark can recover from the checkpoint
   - Instead of recomputing from the original data source, it starts from the checkpoint
   - This significantly reduces recovery time for long-running iterative processes

3. **Memory Management**:
   - Checkpointed RDDs can be stored on disk, freeing memory
   - Useful for iterative algorithms (e.g., machine learning, graph algorithms)
   - Prevents memory pressure in long-running jobs

4. **Performance Optimization**:
   - Breaking lineage reduces the complexity of the execution plan
   - Spark can optimize operations more effectively with shorter lineages
   - Reduces the overhead of tracking transformations

5. **Use Cases**:
   - While loops processing streaming data
   - Recursive RDD transformations
   - Iterative machine learning algorithms
   - Multi-pass data quality improvement (as demonstrated)
    """)
    
    # Demonstrate checkpoint recovery simulation
    print("\nSimulating checkpoint recovery scenario...")
    
    # Create a checkpointed RDD
    checkpointed_rdd = improved_rdd
    checkpointed_rdd.checkpoint()
    
    # Force materialization
    checkpoint_count = checkpointed_rdd.count()
    print(f"✓ Checkpointed RDD materialized: {checkpoint_count:,} rows")
    
    # Simulate recovery: create new RDD from checkpoint location
    # In real failure scenarios, Spark automatically uses checkpoint data
    print("\nIn a real failure scenario:")
    print("  1. Node failure occurs during computation")
    print("  2. Spark detects the failure")
    print("  3. Spark recovers from the last checkpoint")
    print("  4. Computation continues from checkpoint (no full recomputation)")
    print("  5. Significantly faster recovery compared to recomputing from source")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 7: Data Quality Report Generation
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)

    # Convert improved RDD back to DataFrame for final validation

    # Generate comprehensive quality report

    # Final statistics

    print(f"\n" + "=" * 60)

    print(f"  Retention rate: {retention_rate:.2f}%")
    print(f"  Rows removed: {original_count - final_count:,}")
    
    # Column-level statistics
    print(f"\nColumn-level Quality Metrics:")
    for column_name in ["id", "title", "text"]:
        col_stats = improved_df.select(

    # Demonstrate recursive RDD transformation with checkpointing
    def recursive_rdd_processing(rdd, depth=0, max_depth=3):
        """
        Recursive function that processes RDD in multiple passes.
        Uses checkpointing to prevent lineage explosion.
        """
        if depth >= max_depth:
            return rdd
        
        print(f"\nRecursive pass {depth + 1}/{max_depth}")
        
        # Apply transformation
        processed_rdd = rdd.map(lambda row: row)  # Identity transformation (can be replaced with actual logic)
        
        # Checkpoint at each level to prevent deep lineage
        if depth > 0:  # Skip checkpointing at first level
            processed_rdd.checkpoint()
            # Force materialization
            _ = processed_rdd.take(1)
            print(f"  ✓ Checkpointed at depth {depth}")
        
        # Recursive call
        return recursive_rdd_processing(processed_rdd, depth + 1, max_depth)
    
    print("\nDemonstrating recursive RDD processing with checkpointing...")
    sample_rdd = df_source.rdd.sample(False, 0.1, seed=42)  # Sample 10% for demonstration
    recursive_result = recursive_rdd_processing(sample_rdd, max_depth=3)
    recursive_count = recursive_result.count()
    
    print(f"\n✓ Recursive processing completed")
    print(f"  Processed rows: {recursive_count:,}")
    print(f"  Checkpointing prevented lineage explosion in recursive calls")

Task 9: LSEPI & Critical Thinking¶

Introduction¶

The WikiCorpus dataset, derived from Wikipedia articles, presents a fascinating case study in the intersection of open-source knowledge, big data analytics, and ethical computing. While Wikipedia's content is clearly public and freely accessible, the aggregation, transformation, and analytical processing of this corpus through distributed systems like Apache Spark raises deep questions about legal frameworks, social responsibility, ethical data handling, and professional accountability. This analysis examines the multilevel LSEPI implications that emerge when converting Wikipedia's collaborative knowledge into structured datasets for machine learning and analytical purposes.

Legal implications: copyright, licensing, and data provenance¶

Copyright and Licensing Complexity

Wikipedia articles are licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike (CC BY-SA), which theoretically allows redistribution and modification. However, the legal landscape becomes nuanced when considering the WikiCorpus dataset. The alteration process – extracting text, removing markup, and restructuring the content – ​​creates a derivative work that may have a different legal status than the original articles. While CC BY-SA allows derivatives, the ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) pipeline introduces questions about whether a dataset constitutes a "substantial transformation" that could impact licensing obligations.

The legal complexity increases when considering that Wikipedia articles may contain copyrighted material used under fair use provisions. When aggregating 150,000 articles into one repository, the cumulative effect of potential fair use claims becomes legally unclear.

Data provenance and chain of custody

In the context of big data analytics, maintaining a clear chain of data provenance is legally important, especially for research into regulated industries or requiring audit trails. The WikiCorpus dataset, obtained from Hugging Face, represents a secondary or tertiary source of Wikipedia content. This multi-hop data lineage creates challenges for legal compliance: if a Wikipedia article is later found to contain offensive content, copyrighted material, or a privacy violation, determining liability in the data pipeline becomes complex.

The ETL stage raises these concerns. When Spark Transform modifies, filters, or aggregates Wikipedia content, the original context and attribution may be lost. Legal frameworks such as the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and various data protection laws require organizations to maintain records of data processing activities. For WikiCorpus, this means tracking not only source articles, but every change applied during the Spark pipeline – a requirement that challenges traditional big data practices focused on performance over auditability.

Social Implications: Knowledge Representation and Bias Amplification¶

Geographic and linguistic bias

Wikipedia's content is not evenly distributed across languages, cultures, or geographic regions. The English Wikipedia, from which WikiCorpus is derived, disproportionately represents Western perspectives, developed countries, and English-speaking cultures. When this corpus is used for training language models, sentiment analysis, or knowledge extraction systems, these biases become embedded in downstream applications, potentially maintaining and exacerbating existing knowledge gaps.

Editorial Bias and Power Structures

Wikipedia's collaborative editing model, while democratic in theory, exhibits significant power imbalances in practice. A small percentage of editors control the bulk of the content, and these editors are predominantly from developed countries, male, and well educated. When WikiCorpus is processed through Spark pipelines that weight articles based on length, citation count, or edit frequency, these editorial biases become structural features of the dataset.

The social consequence is that some perspectives – particularly those of marginalized communities, non-academic knowledge holders and oral traditions – are systematically under-represented. Big data analytics relying on WikiCorpus may inadvertently reinforce these power structures by treating Wikipedia's representation as objective truth rather than as a socially constructed knowledge base with inherent biases.

Temporal bias and historical representation

Wikipedia articles are living documents, constantly edited and updated. The WikiCorpus dataset represents a snapshot in time, capturing knowledge as it existed at the time of extraction. This temporal bias has social implications: historical events, scientific understanding, and cultural narratives evolve, but frozen repositories may retain outdated or changed information.

When analytical models trained on WikiCorpus are deployed, they may generate insights based on historical knowledge that no longer reflect current understanding. In fields such as medicine, climate science, or social policy, this temporal bias can have serious social consequences, potentially influencing decisions based on outdated information.

Ethical Implications: Privacy, Consent, and Algorithmic Accountability¶

Privacy Concerns in Collaborative Content

While Wikipedia articles are public, the individuals mentioned in them—biographical subjects, cited researchers, referenced public figures—may not have consented to have their information collected into a machine learning dataset. The ETL process extracts and structures this information in ways that enable new forms of analysis, such as relationship extraction, entity linking, or biographical profiling, that go beyond the original context of Wikipedia articles.

Ethical concerns are particularly acute for individuals who are the subject of Wikipedia articles but have not chosen to become public figures. When the Wikicorpus is used to train models that can generate biographical summaries, predict career trajectories, or analyze social networks, the privacy implications extend into new analytical domains beyond the original Wikipedia context.

Informed Consent and Data Subject Rights

Modern data protection frameworks, notably the GDPR, establish rights for data subjects including the right to erasure, the right to rectification and the right to object to processing. However, the distributed nature of WikiCorpus and its processing through the Spark cluster creates practical challenges for the exercise of these rights. If an individual requests removal of their information from a WikiCorpus-derived analytic system, it becomes technically and ethically complex to identify and remove all instances in states with distributed data partitioning, cached RDDs, and checkpoints.

The ethical question extends to whether Wikipedia's contributors – the volunteers who write and edit articles – have any rights over how their collaborative work is used commercially or to race.

Algorithmic Responsiveness and Model Interpretation

When the WikiCorpus is used to train machine learning models, the complexity of Spark-based feature engineering and the ambiguity of the resulting models create accountability challenges. If a model trained on the WikiCorpus makes biased predictions or produces harmful content, it becomes difficult to trace decisions on specific Wikipedia articles or changes. The distributed nature of Spark processing, with data divided across nodes and transformations applied in parallel, makes interpretation more complex.

This lack of algorithmic accountability has ethical implications for fairness, transparency, and recourse. If a WikiCorpus-trained model discriminates against certain groups or produces misinformation, affected individuals may have limited ability to understand why or seek redress, especially when the model's behavior emerges from complex interactions between thousands of articles and sophisticated feature engineering.

Business Implications: Data Science Ethics and Best Practices¶

Professional Responsibility in Data Curation

Data scientists working with WikiCorpus bear a professional responsibility to understand and communicate the dataset's limitations, biases, and ethical considerations. The ease of loading WikiCorpus from Hugging Face – often a single line of code – can obscure the complex LSEPI ideas underlying the dataset. Business ethics require practitioners to perform due diligence on data sources, understand licensing barriers, and assess bias implications before deploying analytical systems.

The business challenge is increased by the scale and complexity of big data systems. 150,000 articles are processed in distributed clusters in a Spark environment

Reproducibility and Scientific Integrity

The WikiCorpus dataset, like many big data resources, presents challenges for scientific reproducibility. Wikipedia articles change over time, and different citations may yield different content. When research papers report results based on the WikiCorpus, the specific version, extraction date, and preprocessing steps become important for reproducibility. However, the complexity of Spark pipelines – with caching, checkpointing, and distributed changes – can make exact reproduction difficult.

Business integrity requires clear documentation of data provenance, transformation steps, and version information. However, the performance-focused culture of big data engineering often prioritizes optimization over documentation, creating a tension between professional best practices and practical implementation barriers.

Interdisciplinary Collaboration and Ethical Oversight

The LSEPI implications of WikiCorpus extend beyond the technical field of data science to legal, social science, and ethics expertise. Professional practice requires collaboration with domain experts who can assess copyright implications, identify social biases, and evaluate ethical concerns. However, the technical complexity of Spark-based systems can create barriers to effective interdisciplinary collaboration, as non-technical stakeholders may have difficulty understanding how data changes affect LSEPI considerations.

Professional development in big data analytics should include training in LSEPI awareness, interdisciplinary collaboration, and ethical decision-making frameworks. The field needs mechanisms for ongoing ethical oversight, especially as analytical applications of datasets like WikiCorpus have become more sophisticated and influential.

if 'df_wikicorpus_validated' in globals() and df_wikicorpus_validated is not None:
    df_source = df_wikicorpus_validated
    print("\n✓ Using validated wikicorpus dataframe from Task 18")
elif 'df_wikicorpus' in globals() and df_wikicorpus is not None:
    df_source = df_wikicorpus
    print("\n✓ Using cleaned wikicorpus dataframe")
else:
    print("\n✗ Error: No dataframe available. Please load and clean the dataset first.")
    df_source = None

if df_source is not None:
    # ============================================
    # STEP 1: Prepare Data for Window Functions
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 1: Preparing Data for Window Function Analysis")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    # Create derived features for window function analysis
    print("\nCreating derived features using DataFrame operations...")
    
    df_prepared = df_source.select(
        col("id"),
        col("title"),
        col("text"),
        # Text length metrics
        length(col("text")).alias("text_length"),
        length(col("title")).alias("title_length"),
        # Word count (using split and size - DataFrame native functions)
        size(split(col("text"), "\\s+")).alias("word_count"),
        size(split(col("title"), "\\s+")).alias("title_word_count"),
        # Categorize articles by length for partitioning
        when(length(col("text")) < 1000, "short")
        .when(length(col("text")) < 5000, "medium")
        .when(length(col("text")) < 20000, "long")
        .otherwise("very_long")
        .alias("text_length_category"),
        # Categorize by title length
        when(length(col("title")) < 20, "short_title")
        .when(length(col("title")) < 40, "medium_title")
        .otherwise("long_title")
        .alias("title_length_category")
    )
    
    # Cache for performance
    df_prepared.cache()
    
    total_rows = df_prepared.count()
    print(f"\n✓ Data preparation completed")
    print(f"  Total articles: {total_rows:,}")
    print(f"  Features created: text_length, word_count, length_categories")
    
    # Show distribution of categories
    print("\nCategory Distribution:")
    category_dist = df_prepared.groupBy("text_length_category").agg(
        F.count("*").alias("count")
    ).orderBy("text_length_category").collect()
    
    for row in category_dist:
        percentage = (row['count'] / total_rows * 100) if total_rows > 0 else 0
        print(f"  {row['text_length_category']}: {row['count']:,} articles ({percentage:.2f}%)")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 2: Window Function 1 - Cumulative Word Count with Multiple Partitions
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 2: Window Function 1 - Cumulative Word Count Analysis")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    print("\nImplementing cumulative word count with partitioning by:")
    print("  • text_length_category (short, medium, long, very_long)")
    print("  • title_length_category (short_title, medium_title, long_title)")
    
    # Define window specification with multiple partitions
    # This creates a complex partitioning scheme requiring data shuffling
    window_spec_1 = Window.partitionBy("text_length_category", "title_length_category") \
        .orderBy("word_count") \
        .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)
    
    # Apply window function: cumulative word count within each partition
    df_with_cumulative = df_prepared.withColumn(
        "cumulative_word_count",
        spark_sum("word_count").over(window_spec_1)
    ).withColumn(
        "running_avg_word_count",
        avg("word_count").over(window_spec_1)
    ).withColumn(
        "word_count_rank",
        rank().over(window_spec_1)
    )
    
    print("\n✓ Window Function 1 applied:")
    print("  • cumulative_word_count: Running sum of words within partition")
    print("  • running_avg_word_count: Running average within partition")
    print("  • word_count_rank: Rank by word count within partition")
    
    # Show sample results
    print("\nSample results (first 10 rows per partition):")
    df_with_cumulative.select(
        "id", "title_length_category", "text_length_category",
        "word_count", "cumulative_word_count", 
        "running_avg_word_count", "word_count_rank"
    ).orderBy("text_length_category", "title_length_category", "word_count").show(20, truncate=False)
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 3: Window Function 2 - Rank-Based Analysis with Percentile Ranking
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 3: Window Function 2 - Rank-Based Percentile Analysis")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    # Define a more complex window specification
    # Partition by text_length_category, order by text_length descending
    window_spec_2 = Window.partitionBy("text_length_category") \
        .orderBy(col("text_length").desc())
    
    # Apply multiple ranking functions
    df_with_ranking = df_prepared.withColumn(
        "text_length_rank",
        rank().over(window_spec_2)
    ).withColumn(
        "text_length_dense_rank",
        dense_rank().over(window_spec_2)
    ).withColumn(
        "text_length_row_number",
        row_number().over(window_spec_2)
    ).withColumn(
        "text_length_percent_rank",
        percent_rank().over(window_spec_2)
    ).withColumn(
        "text_length_cume_dist",
        cume_dist().over(window_spec_2)
    ).withColumn(
        "text_length_ntile",
        ntile(10).over(window_spec_2)  # Divide into 10 buckets
    ).withColumn(
        "text_length_lead",
        lead("text_length", 1).over(window_spec_2)
    ).withColumn(
        "text_length_lag",
        lag("text_length", 1).over(window_spec_2)
    )
    
    print("\n✓ Window Function 2 applied with multiple ranking functions:")
    print("  • rank(): Standard ranking with gaps")
    print("  • dense_rank(): Ranking without gaps")
    print("  • row_number(): Unique sequential numbering")
    print("  • percent_rank(): Relative rank (0.0 to 1.0)")
    print("  • cume_dist(): Cumulative distribution")
    print("  • ntile(10): Divide into 10 equal groups")
    print("  • lead(): Next value in partition")
    print("  • lag(): Previous value in partition")
    
    # Show sample results
    print("\nSample ranking results (top 15 articles by length within each category):")
    df_with_ranking.select(
        "id", "text_length_category", "text_length",
        "text_length_rank", "text_length_dense_rank", "text_length_row_number",
        "text_length_percent_rank", "text_length_ntile"
    ).orderBy("text_length_category", "text_length_rank").show(20, truncate=False)
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 4: Analyze Execution Plan
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 4: Execution Plan Analysis")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    print("\nAnalyzing execution plan for Window Function 1...")
    print("-" * 60)
    
    # Get execution plan
    plan_1 = df_with_cumulative.explain(True)
    print("\nExecution Plan (Formatted):")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    # Analyze the plan programmatically
    plan_string = df_with_cumulative._jdf.queryExecution().toString()
    
    # Check for shuffling operations
    has_exchange = "Exchange" in plan_string or "exchange" in plan_string.lower()
    has_window = "Window" in plan_string or "window" in plan_string.lower()
    has_sort = "Sort" in plan_string or "sort" in plan_string.lower()
    
    print("\nKey Execution Plan Components:")
    print(f"  • Exchange (Shuffling): {'✓ Present' if has_exchange else '✗ Not found'}")
    print(f"  • Window Operations: {'✓ Present' if has_window else '✗ Not found'}")
    print(f"  • Sort Operations: {'✓ Present' if has_sort else '✗ Not found'}")
    
    print("\nFull Execution Plan:")
    print("-" * 60)
    df_with_cumulative.explain(True)
    
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("Analyzing execution plan for Window Function 2...")
    print("-" * 60)
    
    plan_2 = df_with_ranking.explain(True)
    plan_string_2 = df_with_ranking._jdf.queryExecution().toString()
    
    has_exchange_2 = "Exchange" in plan_string_2 or "exchange" in plan_string_2.lower()
    has_window_2 = "Window" in plan_string_2 or "window" in plan_string_2.lower()
    
    print("\nKey Execution Plan Components:")
    print(f"  • Exchange (Shuffling): {'✓ Present' if has_exchange_2 else '✗ Not found'}")
    print(f"  • Window Operations: {'✓ Present' if has_window_2 else '✗ Not found'}")
    
    print("\nFull Execution Plan:")
    print("-" * 60)
    df_with_ranking.explain(True)
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 5: Discuss Data Movement and Shuffling
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 5: Data Movement and Shuffling Analysis")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    print("""
Understanding Spark's Data Movement for Window Functions:

1. **Partitioning Phase (Shuffling)**:
   - When window functions use PARTITION BY, Spark must reorganize data
   - Articles are redistributed across cluster nodes based on partition keys
   - For Window Function 1: Data is shuffled by (text_length_category, title_length_category)
   - For Window Function 2: Data is shuffled by text_length_category
   - This requires network I/O and is the most expensive operation

2. **Sorting Phase**:
   - After partitioning, data within each partition must be sorted by ORDER BY clause
   - For Window Function 1: Sorted by word_count within each partition
   - For Window Function 2: Sorted by text_length DESC within each partition
   - Sorting happens locally on each node after shuffling

3. **Window Frame Calculation**:
   - Once partitioned and sorted, window functions compute values
   - ROWS BETWEEN defines the frame: unboundedPreceding to currentRow
   - Cumulative calculations (sum, avg) are computed incrementally
   - Ranking functions (rank, dense_rank) compare values within frame

4. **Performance Implications**:
   - Multiple partitions increase shuffling overhead
   - More partition columns = more network traffic
   - ORDER BY requires sorting, adding computational cost
   - Window frames with unboundedPreceding scan all previous rows
    """)
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 6: Performance Comparison
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 6: Performance Comparison - Single vs Multiple Partitions")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    # Test 1: Window function with single partition
    print("\nTest 1: Window function with single partition (no partitioning)")
    window_single = Window.orderBy("word_count")
    
    start_time = time.time()
    df_single_part = df_prepared.withColumn(
        "cumulative_single",
        spark_sum("word_count").over(window_single)
    )
    _ = df_single_part.count()  # Force execution
    time_single = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"  Execution time: {time_single:.2f} seconds")
    print(f"  Shuffling: Minimal (only sorting required)")
    
    # Test 2: Window function with multiple partitions (from Window Function 1)
    print("\nTest 2: Window function with multiple partitions")
    start_time = time.time()
    _ = df_with_cumulative.count()  # Force execution
    time_multi = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"  Execution time: {time_multi:.2f} seconds")
    print(f"  Shuffling: Required (partitioning by 2 columns)")
    
    # Comparison
    if time_multi > time_single:
        overhead = ((time_multi - time_single) / time_single * 100) if time_single > 0 else 0
        print(f"\n  Overhead from multiple partitions: {overhead:.2f}%")
        print(f"  This overhead is due to:")
        print(f"    • Network shuffling to redistribute data")
        print(f"    • Additional sorting within each partition")
        print(f"    • More complex execution plan")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 7: Statistical Analysis Using Window Functions
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 7: Advanced Statistical Analysis with Window Functions")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    # Create a window for moving average (different from cumulative)
    window_moving = Window.partitionBy("text_length_category") \
        .orderBy("word_count") \
        .rowsBetween(-2, 2)  # 5-row moving window (2 before, current, 2 after)
    
    df_statistical = df_prepared.withColumn(
        "moving_avg_5",
        avg("word_count").over(window_moving)
    ).withColumn(
        "moving_sum_5",
        spark_sum("word_count").over(window_moving)
    )
    
    print("\n✓ Applied moving window functions:")
    print("  • moving_avg_5: 5-row moving average (2 before + current + 2 after)")
    print("  • moving_sum_5: 5-row moving sum")
    print("  • Partitioned by text_length_category")
    
    # Show results
    print("\nSample moving window results:")
    df_statistical.select(
        "id", "text_length_category", "word_count",
        "moving_avg_5", "moving_sum_5"
    ).orderBy("text_length_category", "word_count").show(15, truncate=False)
    
    # ============================================
    # SUMMARY
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("TASK 5 SUMMARY: Window Function Optimization")
    print("=" * 60)

============================================================
STEP 5: Data Movement and Shuffling Analysis
============================================================

Understanding Spark's Data Movement for Window Functions:

1. **Partitioning Phase (Shuffling)**:
   - When window functions use PARTITION BY, Spark must reorganize data
   - Articles are redistributed across cluster nodes based on partition keys
   - For Window Function 1: Data is shuffled by (text_length_category, title_length_category)
   - For Window Function 2: Data is shuffled by text_length_category
   - This requires network I/O and is the most expensive operation

2. **Sorting Phase**:
   - After partitioning, data within each partition must be sorted by ORDER BY clause
   - For Window Function 1: Sorted by word_count within each partition
   - For Window Function 2: Sorted by text_length DESC within each partition
   - Sorting happens locally on each node after shuffling

3. **Window Frame Calculation**:
   - Once partitioned and sorted, window functions compute values
   - ROWS BETWEEN defines the frame: unboundedPreceding to currentRow
   - Cumulative calculations (sum, avg) are computed incrementally
   - Ranking functions (rank, dense_rank) compare values within frame

4. **Performance Implications**:
   - Multiple partitions increase shuffling overhead
   - More partition columns = more network traffic
   - ORDER BY requires sorting, adding computational cost
   - Window frames with unboundedPreceding scan all previous rows

STEP 6: Performance Comparison - Single vs Multiple Partitions
============================================================

Test 1: Window function with single partition (no partitioning)
  Execution time: 0.11 seconds
  Shuffling: Minimal (only sorting required)

Test 2: Window function with multiple partitions
  Execution time: 0.18 seconds
  Shuffling: Required (partitioning by 2 columns)

  Overhead from multiple partitions: 60.27%
  This overhead is due to:
    • Network shuffling to redistribute data
    • Additional sorting within each partition
    • More complex execution plan

# ============================================
# Task 11: Statistical Profile Generation with Aggregations
# ============================================

from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.functions import (
    col, count, mean, stddev, min as spark_min, max as spark_max,
    percentile_approx, skewness, kurtosis, collect_list, 
    when, length, size, split
)
import time

print("=" * 60)
print("Task 11: Statistical Profile Generation with Aggregations")
print("=" * 60)

if 'df_wikicorpus_windowed' in globals() and df_wikicorpus_windowed is not None:
    df_source = df_wikicorpus_windowed
elif 'df_wikicorpus_validated' in globals() and df_wikicorpus_validated is not None:
    df_source = df_wikicorpus_validated
elif 'df_wikicorpus' in globals() and df_wikicorpus is not None:
    df_source = df_wikicorpus
else:
    print("Error: No dataframe available")
    df_source = None

if df_source is not None:
    # Prepare numerical and categorical features
    df_stats = df_source.select(
        col("id"),
        col("title"),
        col("text"),
        length(col("text")).alias("text_length"),
        length(col("title")).alias("title_length"),
        size(split(col("text"), "\\s+")).alias("word_count"),
        when(length(col("text")) < 1000, "short")
        .when(length(col("text")) < 5000, "medium")
        .when(length(col("text")) < 20000, "long")
        .otherwise("very_long")
        .alias("text_category")
    )
    
    df_stats.cache()
    total_rows = df_stats.count()
    print(f"\nDataset: {total_rows:,} articles")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 1: Numerical Statistics - Kurtosis and Skewness
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 1: Numerical Statistics - Kurtosis and Skewness")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    start_time = time.time()
    
    numerical_stats = df_stats.agg(
        F.count("*").alias("count"),
        mean("text_length").alias("mean_text_length"),
        stddev("text_length").alias("stddev_text_length"),
        spark_min("text_length").alias("min_text_length"),
        spark_max("text_length").alias("max_text_length"),
        skewness("text_length").alias("skewness_text_length"),
        kurtosis("text_length").alias("kurtosis_text_length"),
        mean("word_count").alias("mean_word_count"),
        stddev("word_count").alias("stddev_word_count"),
        skewness("word_count").alias("skewness_word_count"),
        kurtosis("word_count").alias("kurtosis_word_count")
    ).collect()[0]
    
    stats_time = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"\nExecution time: {stats_time:.2f} seconds")
    print("\nText Length Statistics:")
    print(f"  Count: {numerical_stats['count']:,}")
    print(f"  Mean: {numerical_stats['mean_text_length']:.2f}")
    print(f"  StdDev: {numerical_stats['stddev_text_length']:.2f}")
    print(f"  Min: {numerical_stats['min_text_length']}")
    print(f"  Max: {numerical_stats['max_text_length']}")
    print(f"  Skewness: {numerical_stats['skewness_text_length']:.4f}")
    print(f"  Kurtosis: {numerical_stats['kurtosis_text_length']:.4f}")
    
    print("\nWord Count Statistics:")
    print(f"  Mean: {numerical_stats['mean_word_count']:.2f}")
    print(f"  StdDev: {numerical_stats['stddev_word_count']:.2f}")
    print(f"  Skewness: {numerical_stats['skewness_word_count']:.4f}")
    print(f"  Kurtosis: {numerical_stats['kurtosis_word_count']:.4f}")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 2: Quantile Calculations
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 2: Quantile Calculations")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    start_time = time.time()
    
    quantiles = [0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0]
    quantile_stats = df_stats.agg(
        percentile_approx("text_length", quantiles, 10000).alias("text_length_quantiles"),
        percentile_approx("word_count", quantiles, 10000).alias("word_count_quantiles")
    ).collect()[0]
    
    quantile_time = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"\nExecution time: {quantile_time:.2f} seconds")
    print("\nText Length Quantiles:")
    text_quantiles = quantile_stats['text_length_quantiles']
    for q, val in zip(quantiles, text_quantiles):
        print(f"  {q*100}th percentile: {val:.0f}")
    
    print("\nWord Count Quantiles:")
    word_quantiles = quantile_stats['word_count_quantiles']
    for q, val in zip(quantiles, word_quantiles):
        print(f"  {q*100}th percentile: {val:.0f}")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 3: Mode for Categorical Features
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 3: Mode for Categorical Features")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    start_time = time.time()
    
    category_counts = df_stats.groupBy("text_category").agg(
        count("*").alias("count")
    ).orderBy(col("count").desc()).collect()
    
    mode_time = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"\nExecution time: {mode_time:.2f} seconds")
    print("\nText Category Distribution (Mode calculation):")
    mode_category = category_counts[0]
    print(f"  Mode: {mode_category['text_category']} ({mode_category['count']:,} articles)")
    print("\nFull distribution:")
    for row in category_counts:
        percentage = (row['count'] / total_rows * 100) if total_rows > 0 else 0
        print(f"  {row['text_category']}: {row['count']:,} ({percentage:.2f}%)")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 4: Cost Analysis of Distributed Calculations
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 4: Cost Analysis of Distributed Calculations")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    print("\nExecution Plan Analysis:")
    print("-" * 60)
    
    # Analyze execution plan for numerical stats
    plan_numerical = df_stats.agg(
        skewness("text_length"),
        kurtosis("text_length")
    ).explain(True)
    
    plan_string = df_stats.agg(
        skewness("text_length"),
        kurtosis("text_length")
    )._jdf.queryExecution().toString()
    
    has_exchange = "Exchange" in plan_string or "exchange" in plan_string.lower()
    has_aggregate = "Aggregate" in plan_string or "aggregate" in plan_string.lower()
    
    print("\nNumerical Statistics (Skewness/Kurtosis) Execution Plan:")
    print(f"  Exchange operations: {'Present' if has_exchange else 'Not found'}")
    print(f"  Aggregate operations: {'Present' if has_aggregate else 'Not found'}")
    
    # Analyze quantile calculation
    plan_quantile = df_stats.agg(
        percentile_approx("text_length", [0.5], 10000)
    ).explain(True)
    
    plan_string_q = df_stats.agg(
        percentile_approx("text_length", [0.5], 10000)
    )._jdf.queryExecution().toString()
    
    has_exchange_q = "Exchange" in plan_string_q or "exchange" in plan_string_q.lower()
    
    print("\nQuantile Calculation Execution Plan:")
    print(f"  Exchange operations: {'Present' if has_exchange_q else 'Not found'}")
    
    print("\nCost Analysis:")

# ============================================
# Task 16: One-Hot Encoding and Vector Assembly
# ============================================

from pyspark.ml.feature import StringIndexer, OneHotEncoder, VectorAssembler
from pyspark.ml import Pipeline
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, length, size, split, when
import time

print("=" * 60)
print("Task 16: One-Hot Encoding and Vector Assembly")
print("=" * 60)

if 'df_wikicorpus_windowed' in globals() and df_wikicorpus_windowed is not None:
    df_source = df_wikicorpus_windowed
elif 'df_wikicorpus_validated' in globals() and df_wikicorpus_validated is not None:
    df_source = df_wikicorpus_validated
elif 'df_wikicorpus' in globals() and df_wikicorpus is not None:
    df_source = df_wikicorpus
else:
    print("Error: No dataframe available")
    df_source = None

if df_source is not None:
    # Prepare features for MLlib processing
    df_features = df_source.select(
        col("id"),
        col("title"),
        col("text"),
        length(col("text")).alias("text_length"),
        length(col("title")).alias("title_length"),
        size(split(col("text"), "\\s+")).alias("word_count"),
        when(length(col("text")) < 1000, "short")
        .when(length(col("text")) < 5000, "medium")
        .when(length(col("text")) < 20000, "long")
        .otherwise("very_long")
        .alias("text_category")
    )
    
    df_features.cache()
    total_rows = df_features.count()
    print(f"\nDataset: {total_rows:,} articles")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 1: StringIndexer for Categorical Features
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 1: StringIndexer for Categorical Features")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    start_time = time.time()
    
    string_indexer = StringIndexer(
        inputCol="text_category",
        outputCol="text_category_index",
        handleInvalid="keep"
    )
    
    df_indexed = string_indexer.fit(df_features).transform(df_features)
    
    index_time = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"\nExecution time: {index_time:.2f} seconds")
    
    # Show index mapping
    category_counts = df_indexed.groupBy("text_category", "text_category_index").count().orderBy("text_category_index").collect()
    print("\nCategory to Index Mapping:")
    for row in category_counts:
        print(f"  {row['text_category']}: index {row['text_category_index']:.0f} ({row['count']:,} articles)")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 2: OneHotEncoder for Categorical Features
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 2: OneHotEncoder for Categorical Features")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    start_time = time.time()
    
    one_hot_encoder = OneHotEncoder(
        inputCols=["text_category_index"],
        outputCols=["text_category_encoded"],
        dropLast=False
    )
    
    df_encoded = one_hot_encoder.fit(df_indexed).transform(df_indexed)
    
    encode_time = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"\nExecution time: {encode_time:.2f} seconds")
    
    # Show sample encoded vectors
    sample_encoded = df_encoded.select("text_category", "text_category_index", "text_category_encoded").limit(5).collect()
    print("\nSample Encoded Vectors:")
    for row in sample_encoded:
        print(f"  Category: {row['text_category']}, Index: {row['text_category_index']:.0f}, Encoded: {row['text_category_encoded']}")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 3: VectorAssembler for Feature Assembly
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 3: VectorAssembler for Feature Assembly")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    start_time = time.time()
    
    vector_assembler = VectorAssembler(
        inputCols=["text_length", "title_length", "word_count", "text_category_encoded"],
        outputCol="features"
    )
    
    df_assembled = vector_assembler.transform(df_encoded)
    
    assemble_time = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"\nExecution time: {assemble_time:.2f} seconds")
    
    # Show sample feature vectors
    sample_features = df_assembled.select("text_category", "text_length", "title_length", "word_count", "features").limit(3).collect()
    print("\nSample Feature Vectors:")
    for row in sample_features:
        print(f"  Category: {row['text_category']}, Text Length: {row['text_length']}, Title Length: {row['title_length']}, Word Count: {row['word_count']}")
        print(f"  Feature Vector Size: {len(row['features'])}")
        print(f"  Feature Vector: {row['features']}")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 4: ML Pipeline Integration
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 4: ML Pipeline Integration")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    start_time = time.time()
    
    pipeline = Pipeline(stages=[
        string_indexer,
        one_hot_encoder,
        vector_assembler
    ])
    
    pipeline_model = pipeline.fit(df_features)
    df_final = pipeline_model.transform(df_features)
    
    pipeline_time = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"\nExecution time: {pipeline_time:.2f} seconds")
    
    # Verify pipeline output
    feature_count = df_final.select("features").first()["features"].size
    print(f"\nFeature Vector Dimensions: {feature_count}")
    print(f"  • Numerical features: text_length, title_length, word_count (3)")
    print(f"  • Categorical features: text_category_encoded ({feature_count - 3} dimensions)")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 5: Performance Analysis
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 5: Performance Analysis")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    print("\nTransformer Execution Times:")
    print(f"  StringIndexer: {index_time:.2f}s")
    print(f"  OneHotEncoder: {encode_time:.2f}s")
    print(f"  VectorAssembler: {assemble_time:.2f}s")
    print(f"  Pipeline (combined): {pipeline_time:.2f}s")
    
    # ============================================
    # SUMMARY
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("TASK 16 SUMMARY: One-Hot Encoding and Vector Assembly")
    print("=" * 60)
   
    print("\n✓ Feature Engineering:")
    print(f"  • Numerical features: 3 (text_length, title_length, word_count)")
    print(f"  • Categorical features: {feature_count - 3} (one-hot encoded text_category)")
    print(f"  • Total feature dimensions: {feature_count}")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    # Store for future use
    df_wikicorpus_features = df_final
