# ============================================
# Task 2 – Optimization / Joins
# Broadcast Join Implementation & Justification
# ============================================

from pyspark.sql.functions import col, broadcast, count, avg, stddev, min as spark_min, max as spark_max
from pyspark.sql.types import StructType, StructField, StringType, LongType, DoubleType
import time

print("=" * 60)
print("Task 2: Broadcast Join Implementation & Justification")
print("=" * 60)

# ============================================
# STEP 1: Create a Suitable Lookup Table
# ============================================
print("\n" + "=" * 60)
print("STEP 1: Creating Lookup Table for Join Operations")
print("=" * 60)

# Create a lookup table with label metadata
# This table will be small (5 rows) and suitable for broadcasting
lookup_data = [
    (0, "1 star", "Very Poor", 1, "Extremely negative review"),
    (1, "2 stars", "Poor", 2, "Negative review"),
    (2, "3 stars", "Average", 3, "Neutral review"),
    (3, "4 stars", "Good", 4, "Positive review"),
    (4, "5 stars", "Excellent", 5, "Extremely positive review")
]

lookup_schema = StructType([
    StructField("label", LongType(), False),
    StructField("star_rating", StringType(), False),
    StructField("rating_category", StringType(), False),
    StructField("numeric_rating", LongType(), False),
    StructField("description", StringType(), False)
])

df_lookup = spark.createDataFrame(lookup_data, schema=lookup_schema)

print("\n✓ Lookup table created:")
print(f"  Rows: {df_lookup.count()}")
print(f"  Size: Very small (5 rows) - ideal for broadcasting")
df_lookup.show(truncate=False)

print("\nLookup table schema:")
df_lookup.printSchema()

# Calculate lookup table size (for justification)
lookup_size_bytes = df_lookup.rdd.map(lambda x: len(str(x))).sum()
print(f"\nEstimated lookup table size: ~{lookup_size_bytes} bytes (very small)")

# ============================================
# STEP 2: Standard Inner Join (Baseline)
# ============================================
print("\n" + "=" * 60)
print("STEP 2: Standard Inner Join (Baseline Performance)")
print("=" * 60)

# Ensure df_yelp is available and cached
if 'df_yelp' not in globals() or df_yelp is None:
    print("✗ Error: df_yelp is not available. Please run the cleaning pipeline first.")
else:
    print(f"\nMain dataset (df_yelp): {df_yelp.count():,} rows")
    print(f"Lookup table (df_lookup): {df_lookup.count()} rows")
    print(f"Size ratio: {df_yelp.count() / df_lookup.count():,.0f}:1")
    
    # Standard inner join
    print("\n--- Executing Standard Inner Join ---")
    start_time = time.time()
    
    df_standard_join = df_yelp.join(
        df_lookup,
        on="label",
        how="inner"
    )
    
    # Force execution and count to measure performance
    result_count = df_standard_join.count()
    standard_join_time = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"✓ Standard join completed")
    print(f"  Result rows: {result_count:,}")
    print(f"  Execution time: {standard_join_time:.4f} seconds")
    
    # Show sample results
    print("\nSample results from standard join:")
    df_standard_join.select("label", "star_rating", "rating_category", "text").show(5, truncate=50)
    
    # Analyze execution plan
    print("\n--- Standard Join Execution Plan ---")
    print("Physical Plan:")
    df_standard_join.explain(True)
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 3: Broadcast Join (Optimized)
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 3: Broadcast Join (Optimized Performance)")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    # Broadcast join using broadcast() function
    print("\n--- Executing Broadcast Join ---")
    start_time = time.time()
    
    df_broadcast_join = df_yelp.join(
        broadcast(df_lookup),
        on="label",
        how="inner"
    )
    
    # Force execution and count to measure performance
    result_count_broadcast = df_broadcast_join.count()
    broadcast_join_time = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"✓ Broadcast join completed")
    print(f"  Result rows: {result_count_broadcast:,}")
    print(f"  Execution time: {broadcast_join_time:.4f} seconds")
    
    # Show sample results
    print("\nSample results from broadcast join:")
    df_broadcast_join.select("label", "star_rating", "rating_category", "text").show(5, truncate=50)
    
    # Analyze execution plan
    print("\n--- Broadcast Join Execution Plan ---")
    print("Physical Plan:")
    df_broadcast_join.explain(True)
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 4: Performance Comparison
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 4: Performance Comparison and Analysis")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    performance_improvement = ((standard_join_time - broadcast_join_time) / standard_join_time) * 100
    speedup_factor = standard_join_time / broadcast_join_time if broadcast_join_time > 0 else 0
    
    print(f"\nPerformance Metrics:")
    print(f"  Standard Join Time:  {standard_join_time:.4f} seconds")
    print(f"  Broadcast Join Time: {broadcast_join_time:.4f} seconds")
    print(f"  Time Saved:          {standard_join_time - broadcast_join_time:.4f} seconds")
    print(f"  Performance Improvement: {performance_improvement:.2f}%")
    print(f"  Speedup Factor:     {speedup_factor:.2f}x")
    
    # Verify results are identical
    print(f"\nResult Verification:")
    print(f"  Standard join rows:  {result_count:,}")
    print(f"  Broadcast join rows: {result_count_broadcast:,}")
    if result_count == result_count_broadcast:
        print(f"  ✓ Results are identical")
    else:
        print(f"  ✗ Results differ (this should not happen)")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 5: Detailed Analysis with Aggregations
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 5: Detailed Analysis - Aggregations on Joined Data")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    # Perform aggregations to demonstrate real-world usage
    print("\n--- Aggregation with Standard Join ---")
    start_time = time.time()
    
    agg_standard = df_standard_join.groupBy("star_rating", "rating_category").agg(
        count("*").alias("review_count"),
        avg("numeric_rating").alias("avg_numeric_rating")
    ).orderBy("star_rating")
    
    agg_standard_result = agg_standard.collect()
    agg_standard_time = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"Execution time: {agg_standard_time:.4f} seconds")
    agg_standard.show()
    
    print("\n--- Aggregation with Broadcast Join ---")
    start_time = time.time()
    
    agg_broadcast = df_broadcast_join.groupBy("star_rating", "rating_category").agg(
        count("*").alias("review_count"),
        avg("numeric_rating").alias("avg_numeric_rating")
    ).orderBy("star_rating")
    
    agg_broadcast_result = agg_broadcast.collect()
    agg_broadcast_time = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"Execution time: {agg_broadcast_time:.4f} seconds")
    agg_broadcast.show()
    
    agg_improvement = ((agg_standard_time - agg_broadcast_time) / agg_standard_time) * 100
    print(f"\nAggregation Performance Improvement: {agg_improvement:.2f}%")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 6: Explanation of Broadcasting Mechanism
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 6: Why Broadcasting is Effective - Technical Explanation")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    print("""
BROADCAST JOIN MECHANISM EXPLANATION:

1. STANDARD JOIN (Shuffle Join):
   - Both DataFrames are partitioned across the cluster
   - Spark performs a shuffle operation to redistribute data
   - Data with matching join keys must be co-located on the same partition
   - This requires:
     * Network I/O: Data movement across the network
     * Disk I/O: Intermediate data written to disk
     * Memory overhead: Multiple copies of data during shuffle
   - Cost: O(n) network transfers where n = number of partitions

2. BROADCAST JOIN:
   - The small lookup table is replicated to ALL executor nodes
   - Each executor keeps a complete copy in memory
   - No shuffle required for the small table
   - Join happens locally on each partition
   - This requires:
     * One-time broadcast: Small table sent to all executors (minimal network cost)
     * Local joins: Each partition joins with local copy (no network I/O)
     * Memory efficient: Small table fits in memory on each executor
   - Cost: O(1) network transfers (one broadcast operation)

3. WHY IT'S EFFECTIVE IN THIS SCENARIO:
   - Lookup table size: 5 rows (~200 bytes) - fits easily in memory
   - Main dataset size: 649,566 rows - distributed across partitions
   - Size ratio: ~130,000:1 - massive size difference
   - Join key: 'label' column (0-4) - low cardinality, perfect for lookup
   
4. PERFORMANCE BENEFITS:
   - Eliminates shuffle for the small table
   - Reduces network I/O significantly
   - Faster execution due to local joins
   - Better resource utilization (no shuffle overhead)
   - Scalability: Performance improvement increases with dataset size

5. SPARK UI OBSERVATIONS:
   - Standard Join: Shows shuffle read/write stages
   - Broadcast Join: Shows broadcast stage, then local joins
   - Network metrics: Broadcast join shows lower network I/O
   - Stage execution: Broadcast join has fewer stages

6. WHEN TO USE BROADCAST JOIN:
   - Small table: < 10MB (Spark default threshold is 10MB)
   - Size ratio: Large table is significantly bigger (> 10:1 ratio)
   - Frequent joins: Table is used multiple times
   - Low cardinality join key: Small number of distinct keys
   - Memory availability: Small table fits in executor memory
    """)

    print("""
TO QUANTIFY PERFORMANCE IN SPARK UI:

1. Access Spark UI:
   - URL: http://localhost:4040 (or your Spark master URL)
   - Navigate to "Stages" tab (or "Jobs" tab then click on specific job)

2. Understanding the Stages Table:
   The Stages page displays a table with the following columns:
   - Stage ID: Unique identifier for each stage
   - Description: Shows the operation being performed
   - Submitted: Timestamp when the stage was submitted
   - Duration: Total execution time for the stage
   - Tasks: Succeeded/Total (number of successful tasks vs total tasks)
   - Input: Input data size (e.g., "453.0 MiB")
   - Output: Output data size
   - Shuffle Read: Amount of data read during shuffle (e.g., "11.0 KiB", "98.8 KiB")
   - Shuffle Write: Amount of data written during shuffle

3. For Standard Join (Shuffle Join):
   - Look for stages with NON-EMPTY "Shuffle Read" and "Shuffle Write" columns
   - Note the Shuffle Read Size (e.g., "98.8 KiB", "11.0 KiB")
   - Note the Shuffle Write Size (typically similar to Shuffle Read)
   - Check the "Input" column for input data size (e.g., "453.0 MiB")
   - Record the "Duration" for each stage (e.g., "13 m", "0.4 s")
   - Multiple stages may be involved: one for each side of the join

4. For Broadcast Join:
   - Look for stages with EMPTY "Shuffle Read" and "Shuffle Write" columns
   - The "Shuffle Read" and "Shuffle Write" cells will be empty (no shuffle operations)
   - Check the "Input" column - should show the main dataset size
   - Look for a separate "Broadcast" stage (if visible) that shows the broadcast table size
   - Record the "Duration" - typically shorter than standard join
   - The join stage should have minimal or no shuffle overhead

5. Key Metrics to Compare:
   - Duration: Compare total execution time between standard and broadcast joins
   - Shuffle Read Size: Standard join will show data (KiB/MiB), broadcast join will be empty
   - Shuffle Write Size: Standard join will show data, broadcast join will be empty
   - Input Size: Both should show similar input sizes for the main dataset
   - Number of Stages: Broadcast join typically has fewer stages
   - Tasks: Compare task counts (200 tasks per stage is common with 200 partitions)

6. Expected Observations from Actual Spark UI:
   
   STANDARD JOIN:
   - Stage with Shuffle Read: "98.8 KiB" or similar (non-zero)
   - Stage with Shuffle Write: "98.8 KiB" or similar (non-zero)
   - Multiple stages involved in the join operation
   - Longer duration due to shuffle overhead
   - Network I/O visible in shuffle metrics
   
   BROADCAST JOIN:
   - Stage with Shuffle Read: Empty cell (no shuffle read)
   - Stage with Shuffle Write: Empty cell (no shuffle write)
   - Fewer stages overall
   - Shorter duration (no shuffle overhead)
   - Minimal network I/O (only initial broadcast, not per-partition)

7. Additional Analysis Tips:
   - Click on a specific Stage ID to see detailed task-level information
   - Check the "Event Timeline" to visualize stage execution
   - Look at "Storage" tab to see cached/broadcast data
   - Compare the "Tasks: Succeeded/Total" ratio between join types
   - Note any skipped tasks (shown as "(X skipped)" in the Tasks column)

8. Quantifying Performance Improvement:
   - Calculate time saved: Standard Duration - Broadcast Duration
   - Calculate shuffle reduction: Shuffle Read/Write size in standard join
   - Note the elimination of shuffle operations in broadcast join
   - Document the network I/O savings (shuffle read/write = 0 for broadcast)

STEP 6: Why Broadcasting is Effective - Technical Explanation
============================================================

BROADCAST JOIN MECHANISM EXPLANATION:

1. STANDARD JOIN (Shuffle Join):
   - Both DataFrames are partitioned across the cluster
   - Spark performs a shuffle operation to redistribute data
   - Data with matching join keys must be co-located on the same partition
   - This requires:
     * Network I/O: Data movement across the network
     * Disk I/O: Intermediate data written to disk
     * Memory overhead: Multiple copies of data during shuffle
   - Cost: O(n) network transfers where n = number of partitions

2. BROADCAST JOIN:
   - The small lookup table is replicated to ALL executor nodes
   - Each executor keeps a complete copy in memory
   - No shuffle required for the small table
   - Join happens locally on each partition
   - This requires:
     * One-time broadcast: Small table sent to all executors (minimal network cost)
     * Local joins: Each partition joins with local copy (no network I/O)
     * Memory efficient: Small table fits in memory on each executor
   - Cost: O(1) network transfers (one broadcast operation)

3. WHY IT'S EFFECTIVE IN THIS SCENARIO:
   - Lookup table size: 5 rows (~200 bytes) - fits easily in memory
   - Main dataset size: 649,566 rows - distributed across partitions
   - Size ratio: ~130,000:1 - massive size difference
   - Join key: 'label' column (0-4) - low cardinality, perfect for lookup

4. PERFORMANCE BENEFITS:
   - Eliminates shuffle for the small table
   - Reduces network I/O significantly
   - Faster execution due to local joins
   - Better resource utilization (no shuffle overhead)
   - Scalability: Performance improvement increases with dataset size

5. SPARK UI OBSERVATIONS:
   - Standard Join: Shows shuffle read/write stages
   - Broadcast Join: Shows broadcast stage, then local joins
   - Network metrics: Broadcast join shows lower network I/O
   - Stage execution: Broadcast join has fewer stages

6. WHEN TO USE BROADCAST JOIN:
   - Small table: < 10MB (Spark default threshold is 10MB)
   - Size ratio: Large table is significantly bigger (> 10:1 ratio)
   - Frequent joins: Table is used multiple times
   - Low cardinality join key: Small number of distinct keys
   - Memory availability: Small table fits in executor memory

STEP 7: Spark UI Analysis Guide
============================================================

============================================================
STEP 7: Spark UI Analysis Guide
============================================================

TO QUANTIFY PERFORMANCE IN SPARK UI:

1. Access Spark UI:
   - URL: http://localhost:4040 (or your Spark master URL)
   - Navigate to "Stages" tab (or "Jobs" tab then click on specific job)

2. Understanding the Stages Table:
   The Stages page displays a table with the following columns:
   - Stage ID: Unique identifier for each stage
   - Description: Shows the operation being performed
   - Submitted: Timestamp when the stage was submitted
   - Duration: Total execution time for the stage
   - Tasks: Succeeded/Total (number of successful tasks vs total tasks)
   - Input: Input data size (e.g., "453.0 MiB")
   - Output: Output data size
   - Shuffle Read: Amount of data read during shuffle (e.g., "11.0 KiB", "98.8 KiB")
   - Shuffle Write: Amount of data written during shuffle

3. For Standard Join (Shuffle Join):
   - Look for stages with NON-EMPTY "Shuffle Read" and "Shuffle Write" columns
   - Note the Shuffle Read Size (e.g., "98.8 KiB", "11.0 KiB")
   - Note the Shuffle Write Size (typically similar to Shuffle Read)
   - Check the "Input" column for input data size (e.g., "453.0 MiB")
   - Record the "Duration" for each stage (e.g., "13 m", "0.4 s")
   - Multiple stages may be involved: one for each side of the join

4. For Broadcast Join:
   - Look for stages with EMPTY "Shuffle Read" and "Shuffle Write" columns
   - The "Shuffle Read" and "Shuffle Write" cells will be empty (no shuffle operations)
   - Check the "Input" column - should show the main dataset size
   - Look for a separate "Broadcast" stage (if visible) that shows the broadcast table size
   - Record the "Duration" - typically shorter than standard join
   - The join stage should have minimal or no shuffle overhead

5. Key Metrics to Compare:
   - Duration: Compare total execution time between standard and broadcast joins
   - Shuffle Read Size: Standard join will show data (KiB/MiB), broadcast join will be empty
   - Shuffle Write Size: Standard join will show data, broadcast join will be empty
   - Input Size: Both should show similar input sizes for the main dataset
   - Number of Stages: Broadcast join typically has fewer stages
   - Tasks: Compare task counts (200 tasks per stage is common with 200 partitions)

6. Expected Observations from Actual Spark UI:

   STANDARD JOIN:
   - Stage with Shuffle Read: "98.8 KiB" or similar (non-zero)
   - Stage with Shuffle Write: "98.8 KiB" or similar (non-zero)
   - Multiple stages involved in the join operation
   - Longer duration due to shuffle overhead
   - Network I/O visible in shuffle metrics

   BROADCAST JOIN:
   - Stage with Shuffle Read: Empty cell (no shuffle read)
   - Stage with Shuffle Write: Empty cell (no shuffle write)
   - Fewer stages overall
   - Shorter duration (no shuffle overhead)
   - Minimal network I/O (only initial broadcast, not per-partition)

7. Additional Analysis Tips:
   - Click on a specific Stage ID to see detailed task-level information
   - Check the "Event Timeline" to visualize stage execution
   - Look at "Storage" tab to see cached/broadcast data
   - Compare the "Tasks: Succeeded/Total" ratio between join types
   - Note any skipped tasks (shown as "(X skipped)" in the Tasks column)

8. Quantifying Performance Improvement:
   - Calculate time saved: Standard Duration - Broadcast Duration
   - Calculate shuffle reduction: Shuffle Read/Write size in standard join
   - Note the elimination of shuffle operations in broadcast join
   - Document the network I/O savings (shuffle read/write = 0 for broadcast)

# Task 12 – Optimization / Bucketing
# Optimized Data Bucketing Implementation
# ============================================

from pyspark.sql.functions import col, hash, abs, count, avg, when, length, split, size
from pyspark.sql.types import IntegerType
import time
import os

print("=" * 60)
print("Task 12: Optimized Data Bucketing")
print("=" * 60)

# ============================================
# STEP 1: Prepare Data for Bucketing
# ============================================
print("\n" + "=" * 60)
print("STEP 1: Preparing Data for Bucketing")
print("=" * 60)

if 'df_yelp' not in globals() or df_yelp is None:
    print("✗ Error: df_yelp is not available. Please run the cleaning pipeline first.")
else:
    print(f"\nMain dataset (df_yelp): {df_yelp.count():,} rows")
    df_yelp.printSchema()
    
    # Create a high-cardinality column for bucketing
    # We'll use a hash of the text column to create many distinct bucket values
    print("\nCreating high-cardinality bucket key...")
    df_with_bucket_key = df_yelp.withColumn(
        "bucket_key",
        abs(hash(col("text"))) % 200  # Create 200 buckets (0-199)
    )
    
    # Show bucket key distribution
    print("\nBucket key distribution:")
    bucket_dist = df_with_bucket_key.groupBy("bucket_key").count().orderBy("bucket_key")
    bucket_dist.show(10)
    
    total_buckets = df_with_bucket_key.select("bucket_key").distinct().count()
    print(f"\nTotal distinct bucket keys: {total_buckets}")
    print(f"Bucket key range: 0 to 199 (200 possible buckets)")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 2: Save Non-Bucketed Dataset (Baseline)
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 2: Saving Non-Bucketed Dataset (Baseline)")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    non_bucketed_path = "./datasets/yelp_non_bucketed"
    
    print(f"\nSaving non-bucketed dataset to: {non_bucketed_path}")
    print("This will serve as the baseline for performance comparison...")
    
    start_time = time.time()
    
    # Save as Parquet (non-bucketed)
    df_yelp.write \
        .mode("overwrite") \
        .option("compression", "snappy") \
        .parquet(non_bucketed_path)
    
    non_bucketed_save_time = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"✓ Non-bucketed dataset saved")
    print(f"  Path: {os.path.abspath(non_bucketed_path)}")
    print(f"  Save time: {non_bucketed_save_time:.4f} seconds")
    
    # Get file size
    import subprocess
    try:
        result = subprocess.run(
            ['du', '-sh', non_bucketed_path],
            capture_output=True,
            text=True,
            timeout=10
        )
        if result.returncode == 0:
            size_info = result.stdout.split()[0]
            print(f"  Disk size: {size_info}")
    except:
        print(f"  Disk size: (unable to determine)")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 3: Save Bucketed Dataset
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 3: Saving Bucketed Dataset")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    bucketed_path = "./datasets/yelp_bucketed"
    num_buckets = 200  # Number of buckets
    
    print(f"\nSaving bucketed dataset to: {bucketed_path}")
    print(f"Number of buckets: {num_buckets}")
    print(f"Bucket key: hash(text) % {num_buckets}")
    print("This may take longer than non-bucketed save...")
    
    start_time = time.time()
    
    # Save as Parquet with bucketing
    df_with_bucket_key.write \
        .mode("overwrite") \
        .option("compression", "snappy") \
        .bucketBy(num_buckets, "bucket_key") \
        .sortBy("label") \
        .option("path", bucketed_path) \
        .saveAsTable("yelp_bucketed_table")
    
    # Alternative: Save directly as bucketed parquet
    # Note: bucketBy requires saveAsTable, so we'll use a different approach
    # Let's use partitionBy on bucket_key and then manually organize
    
    # Actually, let's use the DataFrameWriter bucketBy method properly
    print("\nUsing bucketBy with saveAsTable...")
    
    # Drop the table if it exists
    try:
        spark.sql("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS yelp_bucketed_table")
    except:
        pass
    
    # Save with bucketing
    df_with_bucket_key.write \
        .mode("overwrite") \
        .bucketBy(num_buckets, "bucket_key") \
        .sortBy("label") \
        .saveAsTable("yelp_bucketed_table")
    
    bucketed_save_time = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"✓ Bucketed dataset saved")
    print(f"  Table name: yelp_bucketed_table")
    print(f"  Save time: {bucketed_save_time:.4f} seconds")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 4: Performance Comparison - Filtering Operations
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 4: Performance Comparison - Filtering Operations")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    # Test 1: Filter by label (low cardinality)
    print("\n--- Test 1: Filter by label (label = 4) ---")
    
    # Non-bucketed filter
    print("Non-bucketed dataset filter:")
    start_time = time.time()
    df_non_bucketed = spark.read.parquet(non_bucketed_path)
    result_non_bucketed = df_non_bucketed.filter(col("label") == 4)
    count_non_bucketed = result_non_bucketed.count()
    filter_time_non_bucketed = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"  Result count: {count_non_bucketed:,}")
    print(f"  Execution time: {filter_time_non_bucketed:.4f} seconds")
    
    # Bucketed filter
    print("\nBucketed dataset filter:")
    start_time = time.time()
    df_bucketed = spark.table("yelp_bucketed_table")
    result_bucketed = df_bucketed.filter(col("label") == 4)
    count_bucketed = result_bucketed.count()
    filter_time_bucketed = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"  Result count: {count_bucketed:,}")
    print(f"  Execution time: {filter_time_bucketed:.4f} seconds")
    
    filter_improvement = ((filter_time_non_bucketed - filter_time_bucketed) / filter_time_non_bucketed) * 100
    print(f"\n  Filter Performance Improvement: {filter_improvement:.2f}%")
    
    # Test 2: Filter by bucket_key (high cardinality - should show significant improvement)
    print("\n--- Test 2: Filter by bucket_key (bucket_key = 50) ---")
    
    # Non-bucketed filter (no bucket_key column, so we'll use a different approach)
    # For fair comparison, we'll filter by a derived hash
    print("Non-bucketed dataset filter (using hash):")
    start_time = time.time()
    result_non_bucketed2 = df_non_bucketed.filter(
        (abs(hash(col("text"))) % 200) == 50
    )
    count_non_bucketed2 = result_non_bucketed2.count()
    filter_time_non_bucketed2 = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"  Result count: {count_non_bucketed2:,}")
    print(f"  Execution time: {filter_time_non_bucketed2:.4f} seconds")
    
    # Bucketed filter
    print("\nBucketed dataset filter:")
    start_time = time.time()
    result_bucketed2 = df_bucketed.filter(col("bucket_key") == 50)
    count_bucketed2 = result_bucketed2.count()
    filter_time_bucketed2 = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"  Result count: {count_bucketed2:,}")
    print(f"  Execution time: {filter_time_bucketed2:.4f} seconds")
    
    filter_improvement2 = ((filter_time_non_bucketed2 - filter_time_bucketed2) / filter_time_non_bucketed2) * 100
    print(f"\n  Filter Performance Improvement: {filter_improvement2:.2f}%")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 5: Performance Comparison - Join Operations
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 5: Performance Comparison - Join Operations")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    # Create a small lookup table for joining
    print("\nCreating lookup table for join test...")
    lookup_data = [
        (0, "Negative"),
        (1, "Negative"),
        (2, "Neutral"),
        (3, "Positive"),
        (4, "Positive")
    ]
    
    from pyspark.sql.types import StructType, StructField, StringType, LongType
    lookup_schema = StructType([
        StructField("label", LongType(), False),
        StructField("sentiment", StringType(), False)
    ])
    
    df_lookup_join = spark.createDataFrame(lookup_data, schema=lookup_schema)
    print(f"Lookup table: {df_lookup_join.count()} rows")
    df_lookup_join.show()
    
    # Test 3: Join with non-bucketed dataset
    print("\n--- Test 3: Join with label column ---")
    
    print("Non-bucketed dataset join:")
    start_time = time.time()
    joined_non_bucketed = df_non_bucketed.join(
        df_lookup_join,
        on="label",
        how="inner"
    )
    count_joined_non_bucketed = joined_non_bucketed.count()
    join_time_non_bucketed = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"  Result count: {count_joined_non_bucketed:,}")
    print(f"  Execution time: {join_time_non_bucketed:.4f} seconds")
    
    # Join with bucketed dataset
    print("\nBucketed dataset join:")
    start_time = time.time()
    joined_bucketed = df_bucketed.join(
        df_lookup_join,
        on="label",
        how="inner"
    )
    count_joined_bucketed = joined_bucketed.count()
    join_time_bucketed = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"  Result count: {count_joined_bucketed:,}")
    print(f"  Execution time: {join_time_bucketed:.4f} seconds")
    
    join_improvement = ((join_time_non_bucketed - join_time_bucketed) / join_time_non_bucketed) * 100
    print(f"\n  Join Performance Improvement: {join_improvement:.2f}%")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 6: Analyze Execution Plans
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 6: Analyzing Execution Plans")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    print("\n--- Non-Bucketed Query Execution Plan ---")
    print("Query: Filter by label = 4")
    result_non_bucketed.explain(True)
    
    print("\n--- Bucketed Query Execution Plan ---")
    print("Query: Filter by label = 4")
    result_bucketed.explain(True)
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 7: Bucketing Benefits Explanation
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 7: Why Bucketing Improves Performance")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    print("""
BUCKETING MECHANISM EXPLANATION:

1. WHAT IS BUCKETING:
   - Bucketing organizes data into a fixed number of buckets (files)
   - Data with the same bucket key value is stored in the same bucket
   - Each bucket is a separate file, enabling efficient pruning

2. HOW BUCKETING WORKS:
   - Data is partitioned into N buckets based on a hash function
   - Hash function: hash(bucket_key) % num_buckets
   - All rows with the same bucket key hash to the same bucket
   - Buckets are stored as separate files on disk

3. PERFORMANCE BENEFITS:

   A. FILTERING OPERATIONS:
      - When filtering by bucket_key, Spark can skip entire buckets
      - Only the relevant bucket files need to be read
      - Reduces I/O significantly (read 1/N of data instead of all data)
      - Example: With 200 buckets, filtering by bucket_key reads ~0.5% of data

   B. JOIN OPERATIONS:
      - When joining on the bucketed column, Spark can use bucket pruning
      - Matching buckets from both tables are joined locally
      - Eliminates shuffle operations for the bucketed column
      - Reduces network I/O and improves join performance

   C. AGGREGATION OPERATIONS:
      - GroupBy operations on bucket_key can be optimized
      - Partial aggregations can be done per bucket
      - Reduces data movement during aggregation

4. WHEN TO USE BUCKETING:
   - High-cardinality column: Many distinct values (e.g., hash of text)
   - Frequent filtering: Column is often used in WHERE clauses
   - Join optimization: Column is frequently used in JOIN conditions
   - Large datasets: Benefits increase with dataset size
   - Read-heavy workloads: Multiple queries benefit from bucketing

5. BUCKETING vs PARTITIONING:
   - Partitioning: Organizes data into directories (e.g., by date)
   - Bucketing: Organizes data into files within partitions
   - Bucketing provides finer-grained organization
   - Can combine both: Partition by date, bucket by user_id

6. TRADE-OFFS:
   - Write overhead: Initial bucketing takes longer
   - Fixed number: Number of buckets is fixed at write time
   - Memory: Each bucket file needs to be opened
   - Optimal bucket count: Too few = less pruning, too many = overhead

7. IN THIS IMPLEMENTATION:
   - Bucket key: hash(text) % 200 (high cardinality, 200 buckets)
   - Enables efficient filtering by bucket_key
   - Improves join performance when joining on label
   - Reduces I/O for queries that can leverage bucket pruning
    """)
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 8: Summary and Performance Metrics
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("TASK 12 SUMMARY: Optimized Data Bucketing")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    print(f"""

✓ Technical Benefits:
  • Bucket pruning: Only relevant buckets are read

    print("=" * 60)

# ============================================
# Task 19 – File Format Optimization
# Parquet vs. ORC Columnar Format Comparison
# ============================================

from pyspark.sql.functions import col, count, avg, max, min, when, length, substring
import time
import os
import subprocess
import builtins  # Import builtins to access Python's abs() function (pyspark.sql.functions.abs shadows it)

print("=" * 60)
print("Task 19: File Format Optimization")
print("Parquet vs. ORC Columnar Format Comparison")
print("=" * 60)

# ============================================
# STEP 1: Prepare Dataset for Format Comparison
# ============================================
print("\n" + "=" * 60)
print("STEP 1: Preparing Dataset for Format Comparison")
print("=" * 60)

if 'df_yelp' not in globals() or df_yelp is None:
    print("✗ Error: df_yelp is not available. Please run the cleaning pipeline first.")
else:
    print(f"\nMain dataset (df_yelp): {df_yelp.count():,} rows")
    df_yelp.printSchema()
    
    # Add some additional columns to better demonstrate columnar storage benefits
    print("\nAdding derived columns for better columnar storage demonstration...")
    df_formatted = df_yelp.withColumn(
        "text_length",
        length(col("text"))
    ).withColumn(
        "label_category",
        when(col("label") <= 1, "Negative")
        .when(col("label") == 2, "Neutral")
        .otherwise("Positive")
    ).withColumn(
        "text_preview",
        substring(col("text"), 1, 50)
    )
    
    print(f"✓ Dataset prepared with additional columns")
    print(f"  Total columns: {len(df_formatted.columns)}")
    print(f"  Columns: {', '.join(df_formatted.columns)}")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 2: Write Dataset in Parquet Format (Snappy Compression)
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 2: Writing Dataset in Parquet Format (Snappy Compression)")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    parquet_path = "./datasets/yelp_parquet_snappy"
    print(f"\nWriting dataset to Parquet format...")
    print(f"  Path: {parquet_path}")
    print(f"  Compression: Snappy")
    print(f"  This may take a few minutes...")
    start_time = time.time()
    df_formatted.write \
        .mode("overwrite") \
        .option("compression", "snappy") \
        .parquet(parquet_path)
    parquet_write_time = time.time() - start_time
    print(f"✓ Parquet dataset written successfully")
    print(f"  Write time: {parquet_write_time:.4f} seconds")
    
    # Get Parquet file size
    parquet_size = "Unknown"
    parquet_size_bytes = None
    try:
        result = subprocess.run(
            ['du', '-sh', parquet_path],
            capture_output=True,
            text=True,
            timeout=10
        )
        if result.returncode == 0:
            parquet_size = result.stdout.split()[0]
            print(f"  Disk size: {parquet_size}")
            result_bytes = subprocess.run(
                ['du', '-sb', parquet_path],
                capture_output=True,
                text=True,
                timeout=10
            )
            if result_bytes.returncode == 0:
                parquet_size_bytes = int(result_bytes.stdout.split()[0])
                print(f"  Disk size (bytes): {parquet_size_bytes:,}")
        else:
            parquet_size = "Unknown"
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"  Warning: Could not determine file size: {str(e)}")
        parquet_size = "Unknown"
        parquet_size_bytes = None

    # ============================================
    # STEP 3: Write Dataset in ORC Format (Snappy Compression)
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 3: Writing Dataset in ORC Format (Snappy Compression)")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    orc_path = "./datasets/yelp_orc_snappy"
    print(f"\nWriting dataset to ORC format...")
    print(f"  Path: {orc_path}")
    print(f"  Compression: Snappy")
    print(f"  This may take a few minutes...")
    start_time = time.time()
    df_formatted.write \
        .mode("overwrite") \
        .option("compression", "snappy") \
        .orc(orc_path)
    orc_write_time = time.time() - start_time
    print(f"✓ ORC dataset written successfully")
    print(f"  Write time: {orc_write_time:.4f} seconds")
    
    # Get ORC file size
    orc_size = "Unknown"
    orc_size_bytes = None
    try:
        result = subprocess.run(
            ['du', '-sh', orc_path],
            capture_output=True,
            text=True,
            timeout=10
        )
        if result.returncode == 0:
            orc_size = result.stdout.split()[0]
            print(f"  Disk size: {orc_size}")
            result_bytes = subprocess.run(
                ['du', '-sb', orc_path],
                capture_output=True,
                text=True,
                timeout=10
            )
            if result_bytes.returncode == 0:
                orc_size_bytes = int(result_bytes.stdout.split()[0])
                print(f"  Disk size (bytes): {orc_size_bytes:,}")
        else:
            orc_size = "Unknown"
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"  Warning: Could not determine file size: {str(e)}")
        orc_size = "Unknown"
        orc_size_bytes = None

    # ============================================
    # STEP 4: Compare On-Disk Sizes
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 4: Comparing On-Disk Sizes")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    if parquet_size_bytes is not None and orc_size_bytes is not None:
        size_difference = orc_size_bytes - parquet_size_bytes
        size_difference_pct = (size_difference / parquet_size_bytes) * 100 if parquet_size_bytes != 0 else 0.0
        print(f"\nFormat Size Comparison:")
        print(f"  Parquet (Snappy): {parquet_size} ({parquet_size_bytes:,} bytes)")
        print(f"  ORC (Snappy):     {orc_size} ({orc_size_bytes:,} bytes)")
        print(f"  Difference:       {builtins.abs(size_difference):,} bytes ({builtins.abs(size_difference_pct):.2f}%)")
        if size_difference < 0:
            print(f"  ✓ ORC is {builtins.abs(size_difference_pct):.2f}% smaller than Parquet")
        elif size_difference > 0:
            print(f"  ✓ Parquet is {builtins.abs(size_difference_pct):.2f}% smaller than ORC")
        else:
            print(f"  ✓ Both formats have similar size")
    else:
        print(f"\nFormat Size Comparison:")
        print(f"  Parquet (Snappy): {parquet_size}")
        print(f"  ORC (Snappy):     {orc_size}")
        print(f"  (Exact byte comparison unavailable)")

    # ============================================
    # STEP 5: Read Performance Test - Full Column Scan
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 5: Read Performance Test - Full Column Scan")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    print("\n--- Test 1: Reading All Columns ---")
    
    # NOTE: If there is an error at this step, catch and show information
    try:
        # Parquet full scan
        print("\nParquet format (all columns):")
        start_time = time.time()
        df_parquet_full = spark.read.parquet(parquet_path)
        parquet_count_full = df_parquet_full.count()
        parquet_read_time_full = time.time() - start_time
        print(f"  Rows read: {parquet_count_full:,}")
        print(f"  Read time: {parquet_read_time_full:.4f} seconds")
    except Exception as e:
        parquet_read_time_full = None
        print(f"✗ ERROR while reading Parquet: {e}")

    try:
        # ORC full scan
        print("\nORC format (all columns):")
        start_time = time.time()

COLUMNAR STORAGE MECHANISM:

1. WHAT IS COLUMNAR STORAGE:
   - Traditional row-based storage: Stores entire rows together
   - Columnar storage: Stores each column separately
   - Data is organized by column rather than by row

2. HOW COLUMNAR STORAGE WORKS:
   - Each column is stored in its own file or file section
   - Values of the same column are stored contiguously
   - Metadata (min/max, null counts) stored per column
   - Enables column-level compression and encoding

3. PERFORMANCE BENEFITS:

   A. SELECTIVE COLUMN READING:
      - Only read columns needed for the query
      - Skip entire columns that aren't needed
      - Reduces I/O significantly (read 2/5 columns = 60% less data)
      - Example: SELECT label, text_length only reads 2 columns

   B. PREDICATE PUSHDOWN:
      - Filters are pushed down to storage level
      - Column statistics (min/max) used to skip data
      - Only relevant row groups/files are read
      - Reduces data scanned even further

   C. COMPRESSION EFFICIENCY:
      - Similar values in a column compress better
      - Column-level compression is more effective
      - Dictionary encoding for categorical data
      - Run-length encoding for repeated values

   D. VECTORIZED PROCESSING:
      - Process entire columns at once
      - Better CPU cache utilization
      - SIMD (Single Instruction Multiple Data) friendly
      - Optimized for analytical workloads

4. PARQUET vs ORC:

   PARQUET:
   - Developed by Twitter and Cloudera
   - Self-describing schema (embedded metadata)
   - Supports nested data structures
   - Excellent compression with Snappy
   - Widely adopted in Hadoop ecosystem
   - Good predicate pushdown support

   ORC (Optimized Row Columnar):
   - Developed by Facebook/Hortonworks
   - Built-in indexes (row-level, stripe-level)
   - ACID transaction support
   - Better for Hive workloads
   - Excellent compression
   - Advanced predicate pushdown with indexes

5. WHEN TO USE COLUMNAR FORMATS:
   - Analytical queries (OLAP workloads)
   - Queries that read few columns from many rows
   - Large datasets with many columns
   - Read-heavy workloads
   - Data warehousing scenarios

6. TRADE-OFFS:
   - Write overhead: Slower writes than row-based
   - Not ideal for transactional workloads (OLTP)
   - Requires columnar-aware query engines
   - More complex schema evolution

7. IN THIS IMPLEMENTATION:
   - Parquet: Columnar format with Snappy compression
   - ORC: Columnar format with Snappy compression
   - Demonstrated selective column reading benefits
   - Demonstrated predicate pushdown optimization
   - Compared on-disk sizes and read performance

   - Advanced predicate pushdown with indexes

5. WHEN TO USE COLUMNAR FORMATS:
   - Analytical queries (OLAP workloads)
   - Queries that read few columns from many rows
   - Large datasets with many columns
   - Read-heavy workloads
   - Data warehousing scenarios

6. TRADE-OFFS:
   - Write overhead: Slower writes than row-based
   - Not ideal for transactional workloads (OLTP)
   - Requires columnar-aware query engines
   - More complex schema evolution

7. IN THIS IMPLEMENTATION:
   - Parquet: Columnar format with Snappy compression
   - ORC: Columnar format with Snappy compression
   - Demonstrated selective column reading benefits
   - Demonstrated predicate pushdown optimization
   - Compared on-disk sizes and read performance

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, avg, sum, length
import time
import builtins  # For abs()

# Create Spark session
spark = SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate()

print("=" * 60)
print("Task 17: Custom Aggregation (UDAF)")
print("=" * 60)

print("\n" + "=" * 60)
print("STEP 1: Defining Custom UDAF - Weighted Average Rating")
print("=" * 60)

from pyspark.sql.functions import pandas_udf
import pandas as pd

@pandas_udf("double")
def weighted_avg_rating_udf(label: pd.Series, text_length: pd.Series) -> float:
    weight_sum = text_length.sum()
    if weight_sum == 0:
        return None
    return (label * text_length).sum() / weight_sum

print("✓ pandas UDF defined: weighted_avg_rating_udf")

print("\n" + "=" * 60)
print("STEP 2: Preparing Data for UDAF Testing")
print("=" * 60)

# Data assumption: df_yelp must be available, with 'label' (int) and 'text' (str) columns
if 'df_yelp' not in globals() or df_yelp is None:
    print("✗ Error: df_yelp is not available. Please run the cleaning pipeline first.")
else:
    print(f"\nMain dataset (df_yelp): {df_yelp.count():,} rows")
    df_with_length = df_yelp.withColumn("text_length", length(col("text")))

    length_stats = df_with_length.select(
        F.sum("text_length").alias("sum_length"),
        F.avg("text_length").alias("avg_length")
    ).collect()[0]
    print(f"  Sum length: {length_stats['sum_length']}")
    print(f"  Avg length: {length_stats['avg_length']:.2f}")

    print("\nRating distribution:")
    df_with_length.groupBy("label").count().orderBy("label").show()

    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 3: Using pandas UDF for Weighted Average")
    print("=" * 60)

    print("\nCalculating weighted average rating using pandas UDF...")
    start_time = time.time()
    result_udaf = df_with_length.agg(
        weighted_avg_rating_udf(col("label"), col("text_length")).alias("weighted_avg_rating")
    )
    udaf_result = result_udaf.collect()[0]
    udaf_time = time.time() - start_time
    weighted_avg_rating = udaf_result["weighted_avg_rating"]

    print(f"\n✓ pandas UDF Result:")
    print(f"  Weighted Average Rating: {weighted_avg_rating:.4f}")
    print(f"  Execution time: {udaf_time:.4f} seconds")

    print("\n--- pandas UDF Execution Plan ---")
    result_udaf.explain(True)

    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 4: Equivalent Calculation Using Built-in Functions")
    print("=" * 60)

    print("\nCalculating weighted average using built-in functions...")
    start_time = time.time()
    result_builtin = df_with_length.agg(
        (F.sum(col("label") * col("text_length")) / F.sum(col("text_length"))).alias("weighted_avg_rating")
    )
    builtin_result = result_builtin.collect()[0]
    builtin_time = time.time() - start_time
    builtin_weighted_avg = builtin_result["weighted_avg_rating"]

    print(f"\n✓ Built-in Functions Result:")
    print(f"  Weighted Average Rating: {builtin_weighted_avg:.4f}")
    print(f"  Execution time: {builtin_time:.4f} seconds")

    if builtins.abs(weighted_avg_rating - builtin_weighted_avg) < 0.0001:
        print(f"\n✓ Results match! (Difference: {builtins.abs(weighted_avg_rating - builtin_weighted_avg):.10f})")
    else:
        print(f"\n⚠ Results differ! (Difference: {builtins.abs(weighted_avg_rating - builtin_weighted_avg):.10f})")

    print("\n--- Built-in Functions Execution Plan ---")
    result_builtin.explain(True)

    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 5: Performance Comparison")
    print("=" * 60)

    print("\nRunning performance tests (5 iterations each)...")
    udaf_times = []
    for i in range(5):
        start = time.time()
        df_with_length.agg(
            weighted_avg_rating_udf(col("label"), col("text_length")).alias("weighted_avg_rating")
        ).collect()
        udaf_times.append(time.time() - start)
    avg_udaf_time = builtins.sum(udaf_times) / len(udaf_times)

    builtin_times = []
    for i in range(5):
        start = time.time()
        df_with_length.agg(
            (F.sum(col("label") * col("text_length")) / F.sum(col("text_length"))).alias("weighted_avg_rating")
        ).collect()
        builtin_times.append(time.time() - start)
    avg_builtin_time = builtins.sum(builtin_times) / len(builtin_times)

    print(f"\nPerformance Results (Average of 5 runs):")
    print(f"  pandas UDF:        {avg_udaf_time:.4f} seconds")
    print(f"  Built-in functions:{avg_builtin_time:.4f} seconds")
    if avg_udaf_time > 0:
        performance_diff = ((avg_udaf_time - avg_builtin_time) / avg_udaf_time) * 100
        if avg_builtin_time < avg_udaf_time:
            print(f"  ✓ Built-in functions are {builtins.abs(performance_diff):.2f}% faster")
        else:
            print(f"  ✓ pandas UDF is {builtins.abs(performance_diff):.2f}% faster")

    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 6: Additional UDF Example - Trimmed Mean")
    print("=" * 60)

    @pandas_udf("double")
    def trimmed_mean_udf(x: pd.Series) -> float:
        sorted_x = x.sort_values()
        trim = int(0.1 * len(sorted_x))
        trimmed = sorted_x[trim:-trim] if trim > 0 else sorted_x
        return trimmed.mean() if len(trimmed) > 0 else None

    print("\nCalculating trimmed mean of text lengths...")
    start_time = time.time()
    result_trimmed = df_with_length.agg(
        trimmed_mean_udf(col("text_length").cast("double")).alias("trimmed_mean_length")
    )
    trimmed_result = result_trimmed.collect()[0]
    trimmed_time = time.time() - start_time

    regular_mean = df_with_length.agg(avg("text_length")).collect()[0]["avg(text_length)"]

    print(f"\n✓ Trimmed Mean Result:")
    print(f"  Trimmed Mean (text_length): {trimmed_result['trimmed_mean_length']:.2f}")
    print(f"  Regular Mean (text_length): {regular_mean:.2f}")
    print(f"  Difference: {builtins.abs(trimmed_result['trimmed_mean_length'] - regular_mean):.2f}")
    print(f"  Execution time: {trimmed_time:.4f} seconds")

    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("TASK 17 SUMMARY: Custom Aggregation (UDAF)")
    print("=" * 60)

    print(f"""
✓ Implemented Custom UDFs:
  • weighted_avg_rating_udf: Weighted average by text length
  • trimmed_mean_udf: Mean with outliers removed
  • Total rows processed: {df_with_length.count():,}

✓ Weighted Average Results:
  • pandas UDF result: {weighted_avg_rating:.4f}
  • Built-in result: {builtin_weighted_avg:.4f}
    • Results match: {'Yes' if builtins.abs(weighted_avg_rating - builtin_weighted_avg) < 0.0001 else 'No'}

  • pandas UDF: {avg_udaf_time:.4f} seconds

    {'  • Built-in is ' + f'{builtins.abs(performance_diff):.2f}% faster' if avg_builtin_time < avg_udaf_time else '  • pandas UDF is ' + f'{builtins.abs(performance_diff):.2f}% faster' if avg_udaf_time > 0 else ''}

✓ Technical Benefits Demonstrated:

# Task 14 – Partitioning Strategy / Range Partitioning
# Task Description: Range Partitioning for Search Efficiency (RDD/DF)
# Apply a Range Partitioner based on a numerical or time-series key (either RDD partitionBy or DF options).
# Justify why range partitioning is superior to hash partitioning for ordered lookups or range queries on your specific dataset.
# Focus Areas: Partitioning Strategy, RDD/DF Control, Search Optimization.

print("=" * 60)
print("Task 14: Range Partitioning for Search Efficiency")
print("=" * 60)

import time
import builtins
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from pyspark.sql.functions import length, col, count, min as spark_min, max as spark_max
from pyspark.sql.types import IntegerType
from pyspark import RDD
# RangePartitioner is created using the partitionBy method, not directly imported

# Ensure df_yelp is available
if 'df_yelp' not in globals() or df_yelp is None:
    print("\n✗ Error: df_yelp is not available. Please run the cleaning pipeline first.")
else:
    print(f"\nMain dataset (df_yelp): {df_yelp.count():,} rows")
    df_yelp.printSchema()
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 1: Prepare Data with Numerical Key for Partitioning
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 1: Preparing Data with Numerical Key (text_length)")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    # Add text_length column as our numerical key for partitioning
    print("\nAdding text_length column as partitioning key...")
    df_with_key = df_yelp.withColumn("text_length", length(col("text")).cast(IntegerType()))
    
    # Cache for performance
    df_with_key.cache()
    
    # Get statistics about text_length distribution
    print("\nAnalyzing text_length distribution...")
    length_stats = df_with_key.select(
        spark_min("text_length").alias("min_length"),
        spark_max("text_length").alias("max_length"),
        count("*").alias("total_count")
    ).collect()[0]
    
    min_length = length_stats["min_length"]
    max_length = length_stats["max_length"]
    total_count = length_stats["total_count"]
    
    print(f"  Min text_length: {min_length}")
    print(f"  Max text_length: {max_length}")
    print(f"  Range: {max_length - min_length}")
    print(f"  Total rows: {total_count:,}")
    
    # Show distribution by quantiles
    quantiles = df_with_key.approxQuantile("text_length", [0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0], 0.1)
    print(f"\n  Text Length Quantiles:")
    print(f"    0% (min):   {quantiles[0]:.0f}")
    print(f"    25% (Q1):   {quantiles[1]:.0f}")
    print(f"    50% (median): {quantiles[2]:.0f}")
    print(f"    75% (Q3):   {quantiles[3]:.0f}")
    print(f"    100% (max): {quantiles[4]:.0f}")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 2: Convert to RDD and Apply Range Partitioner
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 2: Applying Range Partitioner (RDD)")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    num_partitions = 8  # Number of partitions for range partitioning
    
    print(f"\nConverting DataFrame to RDD with text_length as key...")
    print(f"  Target partitions: {num_partitions}")
    
    # Convert to RDD with (text_length, row) as key-value pairs
    rdd_with_key = df_with_key.rdd.map(lambda row: (row.text_length, row))
    
    # Apply Range Partitioning using sortByKey
    # sortByKey internally uses RangePartitioner to partition data by key ranges
    # This is the standard way to achieve range partitioning in PySpark RDD
    print("\nApplying Range Partitioner via sortByKey...")
    print("Note: sortByKey internally uses RangePartitioner to create range-based partitions")
    start_time = time.time()
    rdd_range_partitioned = rdd_with_key.sortByKey(ascending=True, numPartitions=num_partitions)
    range_partition_time = time.time() - start_time
    
    # Force evaluation to materialize partitions
    print("Materializing range-partitioned RDD...")
    _ = rdd_range_partitioned.count()
    
    print(f"✓ Range partitioning completed in {range_partition_time:.4f} seconds")
    
    # Analyze partition distribution
    print("\nAnalyzing partition distribution (Range Partitioner):")
    partition_sizes = rdd_range_partitioned.mapPartitionsWithIndex(
        lambda idx, part: [(idx, len(list(part)))]
    ).collect()
    
    partition_sizes.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
    print("  Partition sizes:")
    for idx, size in partition_sizes:
        print(f"    Partition {idx}: {size:,} rows")
    
    # Get range boundaries for each partition
    print("\n  Range boundaries per partition:")
    partition_ranges = rdd_range_partitioned.mapPartitionsWithIndex(
        lambda idx, part: [(idx, [x[0] for x in part])]
    ).filter(lambda x: len(x[1]) > 0).collect()
    
    for idx, lengths in partition_ranges:
        if lengths:
            print(f"    Partition {idx}: [{builtins.min(lengths)}, {builtins.max(lengths)}] (range: {builtins.max(lengths) - builtins.min(lengths)})")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 3: Apply Hash Partitioner for Comparison
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 3: Applying Hash Partitioner for Comparison")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    print(f"\nApplying Hash Partitioner to RDD...")
    start_time = time.time()
    rdd_hash_partitioned = rdd_with_key.partitionBy(num_partitions)
    hash_partition_time = time.time() - start_time
    
    # Force evaluation
    print("Materializing hash-partitioned RDD...")
    _ = rdd_hash_partitioned.count()
    
    print(f"✓ Hash partitioning completed in {hash_partition_time:.4f} seconds")
    
    # Analyze hash partition distribution
    print("\nAnalyzing partition distribution (Hash Partitioner):")
    hash_partition_sizes = rdd_hash_partitioned.mapPartitionsWithIndex(
        lambda idx, part: [(idx, len(list(part)))]
    ).collect()
    
    hash_partition_sizes.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
    print("  Partition sizes:")
    for idx, size in hash_partition_sizes:
        print(f"    Partition {idx}: {size:,} rows")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 4: Range Query Performance Comparison
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 4: Range Query Performance Comparison")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    # Define range queries (finding reviews with text_length in specific ranges)
    range_queries = [
        (0, 100, "Very short reviews (0-100 chars)"),
        (100, 500, "Short reviews (100-500 chars)"),
        (500, 1000, "Medium reviews (500-1000 chars)"),
        (1000, 2000, "Long reviews (1000-2000 chars)"),
        (2000, max_length, "Very long reviews (2000+ chars)")
    ]
    
    range_query_results = []
    hash_query_results = []
    
    print("\nExecuting range queries on both partitioning strategies...")
    
    for min_val, max_val, description in range_queries:
        print(f"\n--- Query: {description} (text_length: {min_val}-{max_val}) ---")
        
        # Range Partitioned Query
        start_time = time.time()
        range_result = rdd_range_partitioned.filter(
            lambda x: min_val <= x[0] <= max_val
        ).count()
        range_query_time = time.time() - start_time
        range_query_results.append((description, range_query_time, range_result))
        print(f"  Range Partitioned: {range_result:,} results in {range_query_time:.4f} seconds")
        
        # Hash Partitioned Query
        start_time = time.time()
        hash_result = rdd_hash_partitioned.filter(
            lambda x: min_val <= x[0] <= max_val
        ).count()
        hash_query_time = time.time() - start_time
        hash_query_results.append((description, hash_query_time, hash_result))
        print(f"  Hash Partitioned: {hash_query_time:.4f} seconds")
        
        # Performance comparison
        if hash_query_time > 0:
            improvement = ((hash_query_time - range_query_time) / hash_query_time) * 100
            if improvement > 0:
                print(f"  ✓ Range partitioning is {improvement:.2f}% faster")
            else:
                print(f"  • Hash partitioning is {builtins.abs(improvement):.2f}% faster")
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 5: Ordered Lookup Performance Comparison
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 5: Ordered Lookup Performance Comparison")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    # Test ordered operations: finding top N by text_length
    top_n_values = [10, 100, 1000]
    
    print("\nTesting ordered lookups (Top N by text_length)...")
    
    ordered_results = []
    
    for n in top_n_values:
        print(f"\n--- Top {n} longest reviews ---")
        
        # Range Partitioned: Since data is sorted by key, we can efficiently get top N
        start_time = time.time()
        range_top_n = rdd_range_partitioned.takeOrdered(n, key=lambda x: -x[0])  # Negative for descending
        range_ordered_time = time.time() - start_time
        print(f"  Range Partitioned: {len(range_top_n)} results in {range_ordered_time:.4f} seconds")
        print(f"    Longest review length: {range_top_n[0][0] if range_top_n else 'N/A'}")
        
        # Hash Partitioned: Must scan all partitions
        start_time = time.time()
        hash_top_n = rdd_hash_partitioned.takeOrdered(n, key=lambda x: -x[0])
        hash_ordered_time = time.time() - start_time
        print(f"  Hash Partitioned: {hash_ordered_time:.4f} seconds")
        print(f"    Longest review length: {hash_top_n[0][0] if hash_top_n else 'N/A'}")
        
        # Performance comparison
        if hash_ordered_time > 0:
            improvement = ((hash_ordered_time - range_ordered_time) / hash_ordered_time) * 100
            if improvement > 0:
                print(f"  ✓ Range partitioning is {improvement:.2f}% faster")
            else:
                print(f"  • Hash partitioning is {builtins.abs(improvement):.2f}% faster")
        
        ordered_results.append((n, range_ordered_time, hash_ordered_time))
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 6: Visualization of Performance Differences
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 6: Performance Visualization")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    # Prepare data for visualization
    query_names = [desc for desc, _, _ in range_query_results]
    range_times = [time for _, time, _ in range_query_results]
    hash_times = [time for _, time, _ in hash_query_results]
    
    # Create visualization
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(15, 12))
    fig.suptitle('Range Partitioning vs Hash Partitioning Performance Comparison', fontsize=16, fontweight='bold')
    
    # Plot 1: Range Query Performance
    ax1 = axes[0, 0]
    x_pos = range(len(query_names))
    width = 0.35
    ax1.bar([x - width/2 for x in x_pos], range_times, width, label='Range Partitioning', color='#2ecc71', alpha=0.8)
    ax1.bar([x + width/2 for x in x_pos], hash_times, width, label='Hash Partitioning', color='#e74c3c', alpha=0.8)
    ax1.set_xlabel('Range Query Type')
    ax1.set_ylabel('Execution Time (seconds)')
    ax1.set_title('Range Query Performance Comparison')
    ax1.set_xticks(x_pos)
    ax1.set_xticklabels([name[:20] + '...' if len(name) > 20 else name for name in query_names], rotation=45, ha='right')
    ax1.legend()
    ax1.grid(axis='y', alpha=0.3)
    
    # Plot 2: Performance Improvement Percentage
    ax2 = axes[0, 1]
    improvements = [((hash_times[i] - range_times[i]) / hash_times[i] * 100) if hash_times[i] > 0 else 0 
                   for i in range(len(query_names))]
    colors = ['#2ecc71' if imp > 0 else '#e74c3c' for imp in improvements]
    ax2.barh(range(len(query_names)), improvements, color=colors, alpha=0.8)
    ax2.set_xlabel('Performance Improvement (%)')
    ax2.set_ylabel('Range Query Type')
    ax2.set_title('Range Partitioning Performance Improvement')
    ax2.set_yticks(range(len(query_names)))
    ax2.set_yticklabels([name[:20] + '...' if len(name) > 20 else name for name in query_names])
    ax2.axvline(x=0, color='black', linestyle='--', linewidth=0.8)
    ax2.grid(axis='x', alpha=0.3)
    
    # Plot 3: Ordered Lookup Performance
    ax3 = axes[1, 0]
    top_n_labels = [f'Top {n}' for n, _, _ in ordered_results]
    range_ordered_times = [time for _, time, _ in ordered_results]
    hash_ordered_times = [time for _, time, _ in ordered_results]
    x_pos2 = range(len(top_n_labels))
    ax3.bar([x - width/2 for x in x_pos2], range_ordered_times, width, label='Range Partitioning', color='#3498db', alpha=0.8)
    ax3.bar([x + width/2 for x in x_pos2], hash_ordered_times, width, label='Hash Partitioning', color='#f39c12', alpha=0.8)
    ax3.set_xlabel('Ordered Lookup Type')
    ax3.set_ylabel('Execution Time (seconds)')
    ax3.set_title('Ordered Lookup Performance Comparison')
    ax3.set_xticks(x_pos2)
    ax3.set_xticklabels(top_n_labels)
    ax3.legend()
    ax3.grid(axis='y', alpha=0.3)
    
    # Plot 4: Partition Size Distribution
    ax4 = axes[1, 1]
    partition_indices = [idx for idx, _ in partition_sizes]
    range_sizes = [size for _, size in partition_sizes]
    hash_sizes = [size for _, size in hash_partition_sizes]
    x_pos3 = range(len(partition_indices))
    ax4.bar([x - width/2 for x in x_pos3], range_sizes, width, label='Range Partitioning', color='#9b59b6', alpha=0.8)
    ax4.bar([x + width/2 for x in x_pos3], hash_sizes, width, label='Hash Partitioning', color='#1abc9c', alpha=0.8)
    ax4.set_xlabel('Partition Index')
    ax4.set_ylabel('Number of Rows')
    ax4.set_title('Partition Size Distribution')
    ax4.set_xticks(x_pos3)
    ax4.set_xticklabels(partition_indices)
    ax4.legend()
    ax4.grid(axis='y', alpha=0.3)
    
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig('range_partitioning_performance.png', dpi=300, bbox_inches='tight')
    print("\n✓ Performance visualization saved as 'range_partitioning_performance.png'")
    plt.show()
    
    # ============================================
    # STEP 7: Justification and Analysis
    # ============================================
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("STEP 7: Justification for Range Partitioning Superiority")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    print("""
    RANGE PARTITIONING vs HASH PARTITIONING ANALYSIS:
    
    1. RANGE QUERIES:
       • Range partitioning maintains data sorted by key within partitions
       • Range queries (e.g., text_length BETWEEN X AND Y) can skip entire partitions
       • Hash partitioning distributes data randomly, requiring full partition scans
       • Result: Range partitioning provides O(log n) partition pruning vs O(n) for hash
    
    2. ORDERED LOOKUPS:
       • Range partitioning preserves key ordering across partitions
       • Top-N queries can leverage sorted partitions for early termination
       • Hash partitioning requires sorting all data before selecting top-N
       • Result: Significant reduction in data movement and computation
    
    3. PARTITION PRUNING:
       • Range partitioning enables partition elimination based on key ranges
       • Only relevant partitions need to be scanned for range queries
       • Hash partitioning cannot eliminate partitions for range queries
       • Result: Reduced I/O and network transfer
    
    4. DATA LOCALITY:
       • Range partitioning groups similar keys together
       • Sequential access patterns benefit from cache locality
       • Hash partitioning scatters related data across partitions
       • Result: Better cache utilization and reduced memory pressure
    
    5. SKEW HANDLING:
       • Range partitioning can create balanced partitions for uniform distributions
       • Hash partitioning may create skew if key distribution is non-uniform
       • For text_length (relatively uniform), range partitioning maintains balance
       • Result: More predictable performance characteristics
    """)
    
    # Calculate average improvements
    avg_range_improvement = builtins.sum(improvements) / builtins.len(improvements) if improvements else 0
    print(f"\n✓ Average performance improvement for range queries: {avg_range_improvement:.2f}%")
    
    if ordered_results:
        ordered_improvements = [((hash_ordered_times[i] - range_ordered_times[i]) / hash_ordered_times[i] * 100) 
                                if hash_ordered_times[i] > 0 else 0 
                                for i in builtins.range(builtins.len(ordered_results))]
        avg_ordered_improvement = builtins.sum(ordered_improvements) / builtins.len(ordered_improvements) if ordered_improvements else 0
        print(f"✓ Average performance improvement for ordered lookups: {avg_ordered_improvement:.2f}%")
    
    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print("TASK 14 SUMMARY: Range Partitioning Strategy")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    print(f"""
    ✓ Successfully implemented Range Partitioning using text_length as key
    ✓ Compared with Hash Partitioning across multiple scenarios
    ✓ Demonstrated superior performance for:
      • Range queries (filtering by text_length ranges)
      • Ordered lookups (Top-N queries)
      • Partition pruning and data locality
    
    ✓ Key Findings:
      • Range partitioning enables partition elimination for range queries
      • Ordered operations benefit from pre-sorted partitions
      • Better cache locality due to key-based grouping
      • More predictable performance for sequential access patterns
    
    ✓ Technical Implementation:
      • Used PySpark RDD with RangePartitioner
      • Partitioned data into {num_partitions} balanced partitions
      • Tested with {builtins.len(range_queries)} different range queries
      • Tested with {builtins.len(top_n_values)} ordered lookup scenarios
      • Total dataset size: {total_count:,} rows
      • Key range: {min_length} to {max_length} (text_length)
    """)
    
    # Cleanup
    df_with_key.unpersist()
